speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a case of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that ministers of the government have repeatedly stated that the anti-inflation legislation before us is not intended to take the place of collective bargaining, and in view of the fact that the Anti-Inflation Board itself in a statement November 7 stated that it did not intend to replace normal bargaining processes, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn):

I am taking immediate steps to check those evictions which are as the result of leaders organizing into tenant groups. I think it is unacceptable. If they wish to organize, there should be absolutely no coercion or pressure on them, and I have taken immediate steps to see that that does not take place. There are occasions, as the hon. member knows, as one learned in the law as I am not, when eviction is quite an appropriate procedure, but we certainly want to see this minimized.

I think the 20 per cent to 30 per cent figure which the hon. member indicated is higher than those which the tenants themselves have indicated of around 17 per cent to 20 per cent, but I am investigating even that at this time. The distinction in control here is whether the provincial

legislation will cover this type of accommodation or whether we will continue to control it ourselves. We are trying to work this out in relation to the provincial legislation. I am certainly looking into these cases individually to make certain that there are no undue increases and that people are not evicted because they are being coerced or because they want to organize to make representations.

subsubtopic: LIMITED DIVIDEND PROJECTS-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CONTROL RENTS AND PREVENT EVICTIONS
speechtext: In view of the fact that, for example, the Ontario legislation restricts increases to 8 per cent and, as I understand it, CMHC officials themselves have said that increases in some of these projects are between 20 per cent and 30 per cent, will the minister endeavour to persuade the Ontario government to include in its legislation these federally financed projects so that there can be some degree of uniformity?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to rise on a question of privilege. I would have liked the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to be present in the House today, but unfortunately he is held back in his riding. I had the opportunity to speak to him last Friday and this morning. I trust he will be back tomorrow and surely will have the opportunity to make comments if he has any.
Last Friday, the Leader of the Opposition linked a statement I allegedly made the night before on television to racism. As a Canadian who has spent his adult life promoting understanding between the two major language groups in Canada as well as solidarity between all the ethnic groups which make up our country, I consider very serious this allegation made by the Leader of the Opposition. I attach importance to it, all the more because I consider the Leader of the Opposition as a man of honour who, in spite of many difficulties known to all, has proved many times his attachment to the same objectives.
I already had the opportunity to tell him personally how I felt about this last Friday. To avoid any misunderstanding about what I may have said last Thursday, I want to table, with leave of the House, a transcript of the interview between Mr. Eric Mailing of CTV News and myself. The text speaks for itself and in my opinion justifies in no way the allegations of the Leader of the Opposition.
On the contrary, the interview rather appears to me like a defence of the most fundamental rights of every citizen and a call to avoid global judgments on the various ethnic groups which are Canada's wealth.
In fact, the only references to racism that may be found in the transcript are in the words of the reporter who interviewed me. I must add that the text does not justify either the introductory comments made by CTV that night.
I would like to raise another point of privilege, Mr. Speaker, concerning a report presented by CBC on the English channel during the 11 o'clock news last Friday.
Mr. Brian Stewart said on that occasion:

A furious Lalonde told reporters in the lobby that the Wasps are out to get the French. He said all Quebec was being smeared by the English media.
The attribution to me of such a statement is a total fabrication and a complete, unadulterated lie. I never said any such thing in any way, shape or form.

Mr. Speaker, on the question of privilege raised by the Minister of Nationsl Health and Welfare, I listened personally to the accusations of racism against the minister on television and on the radio. I think that all parties in this House must admit that if there is one hon. member who is not racist, it is the minister involved here. For instance, he never used his position to make racial discrimination against anyone, whereas I saw this in western Canada, among my good friends of the Progressive Conservative party who say in this House that if the situation is so bad in Canada, it is because of the "French Power" in Ottawa, because of the French Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is not serving Canadian national unity, it is not promoting cooperation either to make charges left and right against anyone, whether a minister, a member of the opposition, or some of my colleagues. I think we must look upon Canada as a country which is ours and in that country rather than devour one another we should at least try to understand one another and serve the best, interests of the people of this country. In that respect, the minister is quite right in blaming CBC because it is nearly always shooting under par and in a mess. It is about time I think that the government as well as opposition members saw in those people, people who are interested-I do not know whether it is out of envy or jealousy- but who are interested in creating discord in the House of Commons instead of reporting accurately and honestly subject matters under consideration and the debates that take place here.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there will be a more important bill before the House than the one we are now considering, at least not this session. I think it is interesting that as far as the government benches are concerned, there are very few members present. It appears they have concluded that no matter whatever arguments may be advanced, when it comes to a vote they will put an end to discussion in connection with this important matter.
My first words must be of congratulation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) for the manner in which he has carried out his ministerial responsibilities. I have always had a very warm regard for his parliamentary capacity and the manner in which he answers questions that are asked of him. The minister smiles at this moment. However, it is difficult for me to understand how a minister with his experience could have introduced legislation of this kind, legislation which has the effect of nullifying the legislative power of parliament and the interpretive and judicial powers of the courts. The bill will go through because it will be forced through by a government which, regardless of the inconsistency of its stand in connection with inflation, has brought about a situation in our country dangerous both to the economy and to society itself.
The minister is sometimes known as the "thumper". I decided to look at the dictionary meaning of that word. I find that a thumper is a person who uses banging and thumping. In other words, it says, to thump is to strike or beat heavily with a blunt instrument such as a club. If that definition were applied legislatively, it would describe what is happening in connection with this matter.
December 1, 1975

I have to say at once that if the vote comes tomorrow, I shall not be here. However, by the time I have finished what I have to say I think the House will be able to conclude how I would have voted had I been here. To make my position abundantly clear, it is not one of politics as such. This is a matter that requires the fullest consideration by parliament. In order to ensure the non-political nature of what I am about to say, I can do no better than to point out that in the other place a speech was delivered on November 24 by a senator who belongs to the Liberal party and is from the city of Toronto, Senator Daniel Lang. As reported at page 1447 of the Senate Debates, he said:
The significance of Canada's absence from the Economic Summit Conference recently held in France should not be overlooked. I suggest it marks a new low point in how Canada is regarded by other nations, and a new low for Canada in the economic world order. From the end of World War II up until recent years, Canada would almost automatically have been included in such a conference.
It is not difficult for senators to remember that in the 1950s our per capita income was the second highest in the world, exceeded only by that of the United States. Today, our per capita income is fifth ranking in the world, behind that of the United States, West Germany, Sweden and Denmark.
It is not difficult to remember that during that same period, Canada enjoyed an international prestige and a small but real military presence, both of which ranked in the world second only to that of the great powers. Now, however, in the eyes of Dr. Luns, the NATO Secretary General, we rank scarcely ahead of Luxembourg, at least so far as our military significance is concerned.
While Canada is still one of the few countries on earth combining natural resources of an immeasurable quantity and a high degree of modern industrialization, our development has now almost come to a stop, and strikes of national significance are paralysing our economy. Last year, only Italy exceeded Canada in time lost as a result of strike actions. It would not be surprising to any of us if we succeeded Italy this year to that dubious distinction.
He then goes on to deal with expenditures:
Canadian governments at all levels have increased their spending by 300 per cent in the last decade; that is, from $14.9 billion in 1964 to $60 billion last year. In terms of the gross national product, that represents an increase from 31 per cent to 39.3 per cent. In other words, Canadian governments today at all levels control close to $40 of every $100 spent on goods and services in the country.
Statistics for 1973, being the latest available, show that such percentage government spending is only exceeded by Sweden and Holland, and statistics for 1975 will, in all likehood, show Canada to be among the highest government spenders in the western world.
Further on in his speech he said:
At the federal level, last June's budget forecast a deficit of $4.3 billion for our next fiscal year. Indeed, it looks like $6 billion, and many economists are predicting that we will reach $7 billion. Canada's federal spending in the first half of the 1975-76 fiscal year is up a whopping 30 per cent over last year. Our net public debt has risen from $18 billion in 1975 to $25 billion in 1976.
Sir, that view from an outstanding Liberal epitomizes the dangerous situation in which Canada finds itself today. I approach this matter by saying that it is the first time I have spoken on the bill. I have studied the legislation in detail and I have come to certain conclusions that I intend to place before this House.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), after two years of "all is well", said in Winnipeg on September 13 that "the Canadian economy is not in very good shape right now" and he warned that "Canada could go down the drain if the economic picture does not improve". Nothing could be
Anti-Inflation Act
more definite than that. Canada's rate of inflation today greatly exceeds that of the United States, where the rate is almost 6 per cent. Trade is down. Productivity is down. Over and over again mention has been made of productivity. For some reason that I do not understand, the productivity council set up under my administration and which did such effective work was abolished as soon as the Liberal party came into power.
Canada's real gross national product is declining. Our growth is almost nil while, according to the lastest report from the statistical branch in the United States, that country's growth has risen 11.2 per cent. Food prices in the United States-along the boundary, at any rate, where many Canadians today do their shopping-are very much lower than they are in Canada.
Why has the government not acted? I will deal with this question in some detail. We are in a very frightening position. For three years the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the party as a whole have been pointing out the danger to Canada of the government's failure to take action. The answer was that it was of no consequence. So serious did the matter become by 1975, however, that finally the Prime Minister did speak up. I remember so well the ridicule heaped on this party and on its leader, yet it won the Liberals an election.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has taken properly, strong objection to anything being said that is not justified by the facts. I point out that the Prime Minister is one of the major wrongdoers in this regard. All through the election he said, "There is nothing to it; it is a matter that does not deserve consideration by Canadians". I remember his speaking in North Battleford, where he read from a speech that was apparently prepared by one of that company or battalion of extra officials who today clutter the offices of the Prime Minister and the Privy Council.
How frightening, Mr. Speaker, it was when he said: "Do you realize how serious the situation is in our country?" Yet he said there was nothing to it. The Conservatives say that there was. "What about the United States?", the Prime Minister asked. "How much worse off are they than we are? They had controls". I point out that their cost of living today is much lower than ours. The Prime Minister then went on to use these immortal words:
Do you realize that in the United States they are gassing their children and killing off their hogs?
I wondered whether we had a modern edition of Herod, but it turned out afterwards that that was in his speech material and he had to point out that he did not really mean children but he meant chickens. That is the sort of thing that went on, Mr. Speaker.
We have endeavoured to be of every assistance to the government, disagreeing as we do with many of the terms of this legislation, by asking that it be restricted to 18 months and not continued through the life of this parliament, because the present plan means that it will be continued until the next election and this will emasculate the economy of Canada and we will be controlled and dominated by bureaucracy.

December 1, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
We also realize, and it is realized by Canadians today, that if action had been taken earlier we would not be in the position in which we are. The Leader of the Opposition asked that the term be restricted to 18 months, but the Prime Minister refused to accede. Why did he do that, having stated he would be willing to accept recommendations and suggestions from the opposition? The only one that was of any consequence he turned down abruptly and cavalierly, substituting a system whereby we might consider the matter at the end of 18 months but not through parliamentary examination.
The Prime Minister asked for co-operation but he denied it through his attitude and his determination to push this legislation through and actually placed the economy of Canada in a strait-jacket dominated by bureaucrats, without regard to any other consideration than their decision that this was the proper course to take through this legislation, intending to have it carried out regardless of any objection raised. The Prime Minister's statements during the election campaign regarding inflation were not true and he could not but have known that they were not true.

He said a freeze would bring only "temporary relief" and that "no form of controls will keep the prices down for any period of time". The Prime Minister in fact said that under no circumstances would we have controls because as soon as controls went on, up would go prices. Strangely enough, there was a complete about-turn in the middle of October. Suddenly that thing which was regarded as the most dangerous economic nonsense was attractive. Suddenly he embraced that which he had always condemned.
What happened during those three weeks which brought about that change in viewpoint? It was not the fact that inflation had become worse, because the latest statistics from Statistics Canada indicate that in September the rate of inflation was 10.2 per cent and in October it was 10.3 per cent. There was no great increase and no change to speak of, yet suddenly he proceeded to disavow everything he had brought before the Canadian people. I have read this bill with care and I spoke about it, giving my own personal views, four days after it came into effect, when speaking to the Canadian Club in Toronto. I said that this bill simply places Canada in a trap. It makes a group of bureaucrats almighty masters in this country. In earlier days they used to sign letters "Your obedient servant". From now on that will be "Your all powerful master". I have never seen in any statute such a conglomeration of despotic bureaucratic powers given to anyone. The Prime Minister was in the cabinet of the late Lester B. Pearson and in one of his books he says, in effect, "I fear the control of bureaucrats who build up little empires around themselves".
The bill in its present form will dethrone freedom far beyond what is necessary in the public interest. It will build up an all-powerful bureaucracy virtually above the law; there is no right of appeal, except in the most limited sense, that in any way will protect Canadians whose rights have been interfered with. No power-hungry person or
December 1, 1975

bureaucrat could ask for greater powers for three years, which will be to the next election. The economy of Canada will be strangled by the political philosophies carried out by bureaucrats virtually above the law.
I do not trust this government. What kind of justice can be expected from a government when, on an appeal now before the Supreme Court of Canada launched by an alleged Mafia group, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the Government of Canada have joined with these individuals in arguing before that court that the crime probe in the province of Quebec is unlawful. Why did the Government of Canada become involved in that? Are the Government of Canada and the Department of Justice afraid that justice will not be done to the underworld? Why add the advice of the Canadian government? At a time when crime is rampant as never before, why should the government argue that what is being done is not within the legislative authority of the Government of Quebec? The court could have found that out without the assistance of counsel for the federal government.
I intend to discuss this legislation very briefly, because if I were to take the time to analyse all the clauses it would involve a great deal of time. First of all, I suggest the question is whether this legislation is constitutional. It could easily be made constitutional by a simple provision in the preamble that an emergency exists, but the government did not dare admit that because it had contended for several years that there was no emergency. The government follows this tenuous trickery that can be found in clause 20. Of all the evasiness I have ever seen, clause 20 is in a class by itself. The Bill of Rights is swept aside, or at least an endeavour is made to sweep it aside, by a declaration under that clause which is not effective, as I see it, because it does not provide specifically, as the Bill of Rights demands, that the Parliament of Canada will in this case abridge the rights providing fundamental freedom under the Bill of Rights. Section 2 of the Canadian Bill of Rights reads as follows:
Every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an Act of the Parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the Canadian Bill of Rights, be so construed and applied as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment or infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized-
Just imagine the field day for the bureaucrats! We do not know what will be in the bill. We do not know what the guidelines will be. We are simply being given a pig in a poke, a skeleton on which there is no flesh and they will flesh it up after the legislation is passed. Under this bill the government will have unlimited right to change the guidelines. The bill provides for the setting up of an antiinflation board which has the power to punish an individual for what he has done that contravenes the guidelines either in fact or in spirit. What greater power can there be than for a board to be able to punish a person for doing something in the spirit and not in actuality?
An administrator is to be appointed who will perform whatever duties are assigned him by the minister. Where the administrator is satisfied that there has been a contravention of the guidelines, or is likely to be, he may proceed to prosecute. If one's rights are trampled on, what appeal does he have? He has an appeal to the hired man of the
Anti-Inflation Act
government, the anti-inflation appeal tribunal. The appeal may be disposed of by a single member or by a panel of three.
Looking at this legislation as a whole, this nation will be under the dictatorship of the Prime Minister or the cabinet to a vritually limitless extent. They do not have to be concerned about any existing laws; they are set aside unless they come within the ambit of the provisions of this skeleton bill. What about appeals? I wish I could go into the detail of the appeals. They are meaningless. They grant no individual the right to protect his rights. The appeal is to the tribunal. There can be an appeal beyond the tribunal only to the Federal Court within such a limited area as to be almost without effectiveness.
If this bill should pass in its present form, the denial of individual rights can well be imagined. Individual rights will be at an end, because whenever the cabinet thinks there ought to be a few more guidelines, changes made in the guidelines or any laws made, it has the power to do so. That power is dangerous to freedom at any time. It can be changed every hour on the hour. What is lawful today under the guidelines can be changed tomorrow and made unlawful.
I shall say a personal word now. As I approach the setting sun of my life I can do no other than stand against the provisions of a bill that will destroy parliament. I stood against the Defence Production Act and Foreign Exchange Act which denied any right to the individual. Finally, after pressure over and over again, a change was made. Mr. Howe said that he would give them the right to sue in the courts, but that that would be restricted so that if they sued and were successful they would receive $1, without costs, because that would uphold the principle.
This legislation will be law; it will be put through. The ranks of the Liberal party are pretty thin today, with 15 or 16 members present in a majority government. They do not want to hear any criticism. This legislation will be passed. I do not want anyone to say I suggested that we in this country should break the law. If it is passed, it will have to be upheld. I have nothing but condemnation for the powerful heads of two or three of the big unions who have threatened to defy the law. That is anarchy. That would be dangerous to the future of Canada. But I would be less than honest if I did not oppose this bill which asks parliament to give the cabinet the power to pass unnamed laws. That is a denial of justice.
I have always been a reader of history, and I know of no example that is contrary to the principle which I now enunciate. My reading of history reveals to me how dangerous it will be, for it is filled with examples which show that when conditions are allowed to worsen to a point when in desperation people will accept arbitrary and authoritarian solutions, democracy ends. The powers that are asked for in this bill made a sham of parliamentary government and deny the rights of all Canadians.
The Prime Minister tried to sell this legislation when he went across the country. I have already mentioned that his credibility is at about zero, whether you consider it in Fahrenheit or in Celsius. He went everywhere across this country. The people sat on their hands. They charged them

Mr. Speaker, I carefully listened while the right hon. member for Prince
December 1, 1975

Albert was upbraiding the government, more especially for its excessive expenditures. On that point, he is perfectly right, but it does not solve the problem stated in Bill C-73. The government had to resort to a rather special propaganda, despatching its ministers throughout the country to tell Canadians, boards of trade, unions, labour and management organizations all about the advantages of Bill C-73 for the Canadian people and the provisions in the bill to control inflation or to avoid its unbearable ravages in the Canadian economy.
We hear many of those ministers depict the world situation and say, for instance, that inflation in Canada is not as serious as in Spain, Vietnam, France and England, as if this were a remedy to the inflation now affecting Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, of course some people are against the bill, oppose it very strongly for various reasons. We are against it because it does not solve anything; it tends to worsen the situation rather than improve it and make consumers still less able to afford current prices. While the Progressive Conservatives fought an electoral campaign calling for the imposition of wage and price controls, today they turn back. They would like the controls to apply for not more than eighteen months. However, their whole campaign was in favour of controls. An objective look at the situation leads one to wonder what the government could do in eighteen months with the present structures of the economic system to arrive at a solution to correct it. In five years from now nothing will be solved. That is the way it will be with Bill C-73. The Progressive Conservatives for their part might have titled it Bill C-74, without solving anything more than the others.
According to NDP members, the controls are not severe enough; they are too flexible. They ought to be made still stronger and all-pervasive, similar to those which nationalization would imply. The government would become the employer, the boss of all economic activities in Canada. The partisans of socialism would be delighted with them. Well, we have examples of a number of socialist states where the cost of living has not been going down, but up like in many non socialist states. I feel that the cost of living in British Columbia is higher than anywhere else in Canada. And yet, a socialist government has been in power in British Columbia for three years already. There has been for many years a socialist government in Saskatchewan, as well as in Manitoba. Although in power at the provincial level, these socialist governments have been unable to prevent inflation from ravaging their provinces, as it does ravage Ontario, Quebec and the remaining provinces.
It is fine always to blame the federal government for everything that happens in Canada. Last night, I was listening to a lecture given on television by Mr. Rene Levesque, the leader of the Quebec separatist party, who was again blaming Ottawa for inflation, for everything that goes wrong, for undeveloped natural resources. And Levesque goes on saying again and again that in a normal country, a normal province, a normal state as the state of Quebec, this and that should be controlled, natural resources should be developed, mines should be nationalized, most of the production and consumption should be
Anti-Inflation Act
nationalized, and then the federalist system would be done for.
Mr. Speaker, Rene Levesque was once the Minister of Economic Affairs or Natural Resources in the province of Quebec. What he advocates today, why did he not do it when he was a Quebec minister? When Quebec Hydro was nationalized in 1962, Mr. Levesque then said: We want to be masters in our own house. That was back in 1962, thirteen years ago. Are we more masters in our own province, Quebec, than we were in 1962? It is worse than ever today. Mr. Levesque, who nationalized electricity, said: We are going to become masters through electric power. Mr. Speaker, they were supposed to standardize electricity rates in the province of Quebec so that consumers would pay less. Today the rates are 10 times higher than they were before the companies were nationalized. That is Rene Levesque's "baby". It is the same Levesque who wants to nationalize the rest of the Quebec economy and who impresses the "suckers" in the province by making them believe that he would do better than those who are in power. What did he do anyway?
Moreover, when he was Minister of Social Affairs, what prevented him from raising pensions? Who prevented him from raising family allowances? Who prevented him from giving assistance to the poor at that time? Mr. Levesque did not say that in 1962 or in 1965, but since he was defeated, now that he is no longer in power, he is capable of everything, whereas while he was a minister, he was incapable and helpless. People who are quite capable when they do not have to give any instructions, but who become quite incapable once in power, we have known some in the past, and Rene Levesque is no exception.
Mr. Speaker, I was saying that the Progressive Conservatives now blame the Liberals for trying to apply restrictions for three years. They would prefer 18 months. Yet, they know full well that within 18 months they would not do any better. That is clear. The system implemented, tolerated and generated is the same for both parties.
Also, objections are raised by the unions. What about Mr. Pepin, of the CNTU, Mr. Laberge, of the QFL, and Char-bonneau, with his goatee, calling for a 24-hour strike, which would bring the workers back to work 24 hours later still suffering from the hardships of Bill C-73? Do those people, i.e. Laberge, Pepin, Charbonneau and Chartrand, explain to their members what would happen if they were in power instead of the present government? What would they do? Some union members are stupid enough to believe that if Pepin, Laberge and Charbonneau were to take power forcibly tomorrow, the worker would be freed. It would be called "power in the hands of the workers", that is precisely when the workers would get kicked, you know where, by guys like Pepin, Laberge and Charbonneau.
Mr. Speaker, we have seen what happened in some European countries because of stirrers of trouble and strike organizers. What happened in Russia as a result of repeated 24-hour general strikes? They led to authoritarian communism. The same thing happened in all socialist countries throughout the world. It happened in Cuba, closer to us. When Castro fought against Batista, he wanted to overthrow exploiters, yes, but in the name of Christianity, of

December 1, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
civilization. But once in power, what did Castro do? He became a notorious communist. Today, when we hear he has built small houses for the workers, we should go and see the police system that exists in Cuba. Go and see the small socialist countries: do the workers hold the power and or is it not rather the union leaders who have become the government? In those countries, no one is free today. That is why the Social Crediters have been saying for a long time now that the day we lose our freedom, we will have put it in the hands of guys like Pepin, Laberge and Charbonneau. When that day comes, our freedoms will have gone forever, and we will never manage to get them back. What do those people want who fight for freedom? They only want to take the liberty of citizens, our own liberties, to seize upon them and then impose on us the dictatorship they have been dreaming of for many years. This is the danger with union leaders. Another has been keeping postal workers on strike for 41 days; a Mr. Parrot said to the workers: Vote against the settlement of the strike. Is Mr. Parrot going to refund the money lost by postal workers in Canada? Some postal workers have lost $2,000 in salary over 41 days. When will they make up for these $2,000? Never. They will not make up for this loss over a hundred years. But Parrot did not lose his salary during the strike. The other union leaders did not lose their salaries. But the head of a family, the postal worker, his wife and his children had only $40 a week for several weeks.
Is this the way to settle the labour problem? Mr. Speaker, and I say it again and again: Just prove to me that a strike is going to settle the labour problem and I shall be the first on the front line with the strikers. But since I know strikes, the end of a strike has always meant the beginning of another. When the contract expires, they still must strike to cancel or renegotiate a contract. Strikes have been known for 30, 40, 50 years. Is the workman better off now than in those days? In my view he is a hundred times worse off than 25 or 30 years ago! That does not mean the government program should be endorsed, far from it. The government program is a kind of law which promotes economic, social and political unrest throughout Canada. In what may? Let me tell you.
I recently asked the right hon. Prime Minister about the notorious Bill C-73.1 asked him how he proposed, when the implementation of the program comes to an end, to balance the consumer's purchasing power with the increased production. I read over the clause of the act which provides for an 8 per cent salary increase to take care of the rising cost of living and which allows 2 per cent indexation and 2 per cent for miscellaneous, making up a total possible increase of 12 per cent. Therefore I told the Prime Minister: The 8 per cent increase is directly included in the cost of production of goods. Surely everybody can see that. The Prime Minister then replied: I have asked him. I then said: Since the worker who will obtain an 8 per cent increase will have to pay taxes on this increase, how will he be able to cope with higher prices, which will not be taxable since the producer or manufacturer or businessman will only have to raise his prices according to what he paid, to what it is costing him, and not a penny more. Therefore, the $800 salary increase will be translated by the retailer and the businessman into an $800 price increase because salaries are a factor of prices. There is no profit for the business-

man. It is simply the additional amount that he must pay for salaries. The Prime Minister says: The worker will have 8 per cent, plus 2 per cent, plus 2 per cent, which means 12 per cent, when prices will only increase by 8 per cent. I am very surprised to learn that the Prime Minister cannot add better than that.
Mr. Speaker, let us consider the example of a citizen whose annual income is $10,000 and let us set present prices at $10,000. This is false because prices are much higher than salaries. Prices are at least 40 per cent higher at the present time, and I am being conservative, not of the Conservative party, but conservative in my figures.
So, what happens? Let us say that this figure of $10,000 is equal to the worker's income, but prices now certainly represent $14,000 whereas the worker only makes $10,000. He is already lagging behind. This government tolerates such a situation. Usually, private enterprise is recognized the right of making profits, but we must fight inflation. We are going to ask manufacturers, businessmen, contractors not to raise their prices more than the increase in real costs. Take the example of the worker who earns $10,000 a year and gets the maximum to which he is entitled. He will get a raise of 8 per cent plus 2 per cent, plus 2 per cent, a total of 12 per cent. This is a $1,200 yearly increase, which means that he will get $11,200. Not only the 8 per cent is included in the prices, but also the 2 per cent. If the government paid the 2 per cent and also the other 2 per cent, I would agree because prices would only go up by 8 per cent. But the government does not pay anything.
The government says: You are entitled to this, but to nothing more. Then the 8 per cent, the 2 per cent, plus the other 2 per cent, are included in the prices, and it adds up to 12 per cent. And 12 per cent of the $10,000 figure I quoted earlier means a price increase to $11,200. So, prices reach $11,200 and the income exactly the same amount. The difference between the two figures is that when a businessman increases his prices by $1,200 according to the increase allowed, it is only a cost increase. It is not an increase in profits, because under Bill C-73, he is not allowed to make a profit on the $1,200 price increase since it is the cost price. On the other hand, the worker who earns $11,200 must pay taxes on his $1,200 increase under the Income Tax Act. He will pay at least $300 in taxes. Let us say 25 per cent. I think that $10,000 a year represents more than 25 per cent. But let us be conservative. When his $300 in taxes are paid, he has only a $900 salary increase left to pay a $1,200 price increase. The consumer has then $300 less than before.
The prime minister did not understand that. He said no: With 12 per cent, he will be able to buy 8 per cent. In fact, it is exactly the opposite. With 9 per cent, he will have to buy 12 per cent. It is impossible for consumers-

The proof is that Pepin and his gang, Laberge in particular, and the good gardian angels who are in those unions, the QFL in particular, are not even able to get along; I learned with much satisfaction at noon that the steel workers strongly object to the 24-hour general strike plan. Gerin-Lajoie said so, then I think that he is the most reasonable and responsible person in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, Jean-Luc Pepin said: the employers are happy to see the wages frozen, but they object to the price freeze. Then, the wage earners of the unions are happy to see the prices frozen but they object to the wage freeze. So, Jean-Luc Pepin told them: Please try to decide what you want. If you want to help us help you we are going to do it but if you are there one against the other all the time, you do not mind if the other guy is squeezed but you do mind if you are squeezed. Everyone is going to have to be squeezed, or nobody will. He was right. If it freezes it must freeze but what will that give? That will give frost. What do you want? We will not know where we are going anymore nor would we have known where to go with the Progressive Conservatives and absolute controls of more than two, three or four years. Not at all. Not with socialization or nationalization.
We say that the gap between prices and the purchasing power is too wide. Here is a specific case. Suppose that prices are $10,000 and income is $10,000. At a certain moment prices increase by $12,000. If you tax the increase in salaries to go and get that amount or distribute that amount the consumer is not better off than he was. A retail discount at the retail price level would have cost a lot less than what the Anti-Inflation Board is now going to cost. It would cost a lot less in bureaucracy across Canada because we could have used the services of Statistics Canada, for

example, which is practically useless, or the services of the governor of the Bank of Canada who sits around all day and does not know whether he must increase interest rates or bring them down who comes to us to try and make us believe that we are better off when the interest rate is higher because that prevents us from having recourse to new credits when everyone is caught at the throat, still being forced to go to banks, credit unions, financial institutions to pay interest rates of 12, 15 per cent.
We say, order a retail discount at the retail price level across Canada after agreement with retailers and the federal government. This would be a 20 per cent discount on prices of $10,000-which would reduce the price to $8,000. The purchasing power is then increased by $2,000 without taking a nickel out of the pocket of the consumer, the small wage earner or the average worker. The balance between products and consumers would then be restored. The other way would be, for example, to increase prices by 8 per cent. That adds to the cost price, you do not make a profit, nothing like that. Instead of saying that if we said to the worker that instead of paying taxes on his income we are going to give in a national dividend to fill the difference that exists between prices and his income. You would have some balance then. But in the present context, far from promoting balance we are increasingly promoting economic imbalance. This is why everyone, all social classes throughout the country, are revolting one against the other or against the government. Reference is made to division and separation. Quebec would be better if separated. In Saskatchewan, they feel their lot would be improved if they were separated. In British Columbia, they think they would be better with the United States than with Canada and while slowly but surely the foundations of a very rich country, one of the greatest in the world, Canada, are eroded, our figures and our accountancy system are not adjusted to our great opportunities.
Instead of a reflected kind of accounting permitted by our physical possibilities, our producing potential, our productivity potential, they try to reduce, to shrink down physical possibilities to figure possibilities, to the financial possibilities the governor of the Bank of Canada and the Banking Association of Canada want to force on us. But labour unions do not tackle that problem. Liberals, Progressive Conservatives totally ignore the existence of such a control. The New Democrats pass judgment on about everything there is, but they propose nothing to put the axe into the current financial system.
This is not the first time, Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I repeat this in this House. As long as we do nothing to put our national accounts system in order, so that figures may be brought to serve the individual, as long as we do nothing in that direction we will have numerous bills such as this one. Because Bill C-73 will be enacted. It will definitely pass, whether we vote for or against it. The government has the majority so the bill will go through this House. It already went through the committee stage. Almost no amendments were accepted.
It will go through the Senate, where the government is also in a majority position. Bill C-73 will be enacted and forced upon the people. The right hon. Prime Minister said so the other night when he announced: "If the present measures are not rigid enough, we will strengthen them."

December 1, 1975
Adjournment Motion
We will use the army if we have to, but the bill will go through, whatever the cost. The fight against inflation is a must. So in order to fight figure-inflation, we are going to fight the Canadian citizens at the same time. Let us crush them! Let us make them suffer as much as we can, in order to pay tribute to a monetary system that someday or other will have to be replaced by something more sensible. The most sensible-those who have been the laughing stock for years-and I mean the Social Credit Party, whether people laugh or not, I say this in earnest: Social Credit is not garbage, it is not a whim thrown the public, it is something reasoned, something serious and well analyzed. A lot of people do not understand it. I referred to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the media, the stations, radio, those people that are always crying: Freedom of the press. People clamour for freedom of the press when that suits them, when their own freedom is at stake, but there is never enough time for reporting what is going on in the House. I noticed in the last few months that when statements are made in the House, CBC and Le Journal de Montreal, Peladeau's baby-I think his name is Peladeau- report that there would be three parties in the House: the Liberal party, the Progressive Conservative party, and the New Democratic party.
Social Crediters take part in all the debates; they are overlooked, ignored and that is what is called freedom of the press. That is the freedom of the press that was kicked out in some socialist countries and when socialism will be established here, all of you, press people, will applaud, you will have won your case and reaped your laurels, but until then and as long as I shall breathe, the dressing-down you will get will be a good one.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-73, to provide for the restraint of profit margins, prices, dividends and compensation in Canada, be read the third time and do pass.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past three years it has been clear that government action is necessary to curb inflation and stop the cost of living from rising at a steadily accelerating rate. In February, 1973, the official opposition in parliament urged the government to introduce a policy of price and income restraints as a means of curbing inflation. As you know, the government refused to follow this suggestion and price and income restraints became the main issue in the general election a year ago. Now the government has finally come to realize that price and income restraints are necessary if inflation is to be brought under control, and has presented its restraint program in the bill we have before us.
Already, many weaknesses in the program have been pointed out by members of the official opposition and others at the meetings of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. Some of these weaknesses have been corrected. Many remain to be corrected before the plan can work effectively to curb inflation. Two things which the government must do are the following: first, reduce the increase in the money supply to a range between 5 per cent and 7'/2 per cent per year. That is the range of increase which has made it possible to reduce inflation in the United States to around 6 per cent per year, half of what it is in this country today; second, keep the increase in government spending to no more than 8 per cent per year during the coming year, thus limiting the increase in government spending to the percentage the government will allow the people of Canada.
As old age pensioners, war veterans and others in need must receive increases equal to the increase in the cost of living, it will be necessary for the government to reduce other increases in expenditure to less than the 8 per cent a year in order to make an over-all limit of 8 per cent possible. Mr. Speaker, I intend to do everything I can to persuade the government to take these necessary steps.
Turning, now, to the situation which confronts us at this moment, I believe the important thing for us to remember is that however imperfect this program is-and we can only hope the government will soon have the good sense to correct its imperfections-it is the only program for controlling inflation which will be presented to this parliament. If the bill is defeated on third reading, the program will cease to exist. The result would be a continuation of the inflationary spiral, our products would continue to be increasingly less competitive with foreign products in both the Canadian and the export markets, and unemployment would rise until we found ourselves in an all-out depression.
December 1, 1975

It is for this reason I intend to vote for the bill and, if it passes, to do everything I can to persuade the people of this country to get behind the program and work in the national interest toward reducing inflation to around 3 per cent per year, the average for the past 65 years during which we have measured inflation in Canada.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on many occasions in the past few weeks we have registered opposition to the bill which is before us for third reading. This afternoon I intend to do so once again on behalf of the New Democratic Party. Our party has long been concerned about the effects of inflation in this country and throughout the world. Spokesmen for this group have at various times made many suggestions as to the steps we should be taking domestically to help bring down the rate of inflation. We have pointed out, too, that it is desirable to seek international agreement on measures to govern inflation since a large part of our own inflation is, as we know, imported. As a trading nation, this is an aspect of the issue we cannot ignore.
As has been stated earlier, we think the bill before us is inequitable since its primary effect will be to control the wages of working people. From this point of view it is a frightening bill and its effect in limiting raises in wages for the working people is likely to be very powerful. Contracts are negotiated in the open. It is easy to control the salaries of, say, teachers in Toronto or potash workers in Saskatchewan. I predict that the wage control aspect of the program will be firmly carried out.
I am concerned about the danger the bill poses to the collective bargaining system. In effect, many trade unions will have to negotiate with the anti-inflation board. I draw the attention of the House to a statement which was made, apparently, by Mr. Pepin over the weekend implying that the offer made by the Toronto school board was higher than the anti-inflation board is prepared to permit. Here is the chairman of the anti-inflation board making a judgment before the collective bargaining process has reached a conclusion. He is intervening in a dispute. These are matters that are of contern to the salaried workers of this country.
This bill is one that will quite adequately control the wages and salaries of workers. On the other hand, it will have very little effect in controlling prices, profits, dividends, professional fees and incomes of people derived from investments and corporate profits. To my mind, one of the prime reasons for bringing in this bill is that the government wanted to dampen down increased wage demands.
During the past year, wage demands have been rising. In 1970, wage and salary increases in this country, as a percentage of national income, stood at 72.8 per cent. In the first half of 1974, wage and salary increases, as a percentage of national income, had dropped to 67 per cent. By the end of 1974, there has been a reversal of that trend and wages and salaries started to go up, representing, as a percentage of national income, 69.4 per cent. By mid-1975, wages and salaries represented 70.8 per cent of national income. In other words, wage and salary earners in this
Anti-Inflation Act
country were starting to get more than their fair share of the national economic pie.
At the same time, business profits and interest fell from 21.1 per cent of national income in 1974 to 20.1 per cent by the middle of 1975. That is why I wonder whether this trend in the economy finally prodded the government into bringing in this bill. A spokesman in the 1974 election campaign said that a bill such as this would be very effective in controlling wages and salaries.
Let me go back to the first attempt of the government to bring in an incomes policy. One saw a similar economic pattern developing in Canada between 1969 and 1970. Wage increases were getting progressively higher and higher. Then suddenly an incomes policy was brought in which affected the wage earners more than prices and profits. I should like to quote a statement made in the "International Labour Review" of December, 1973, by one of the commissioners of the former prices and incomes commission of this country in 1969 and 1970, a fellow named George Haythorne, who explained why the first attempt to control incomes in this country was made. He said:
From 1957 to 1963 the share of Canada's national income going to profits and capital had risen steadily. The situation was reversed in 1964 when labour's share began to rise, a trend which continued until 1970. Given these conditions . .. action to stabilize the economy was clearly required.
Here is a commissioner on the prices and incomes commission in 1969 and 1970 saying that because labour's share of the national income was going up, the government had to do something about it. I suggest we are now in the same situation as we were a few years ago. In fact, in the 1974 election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when talking about the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) to bring in a 90-day freeze followed by some kind of controls, time and again said that that type of program in essence would be a wage control policy. At this third reading stage I want to put on record a quotation from the Toronto Star which reported a meeting that the Prime Minister had in Timmins on June 28 as follows:
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau maintained his onslaught on Conservative prices and incomes restraint policies before a large noon hour crowd here yesterday.
Mr. Trudeau said the proposed 90-day freeze, followed by up to two years of controls, would take vast numbers of bureaucrats to administer. Even then, it wouldn't work. He said: "You can't freeze executive salaries and dividends because there are too many loopholes to squeeze through".
Mr. Trudeau said Conservative leader Robert Stanfield had already said he would not freeze the prices of farm produce and fish. He could not freeze the prices of U S. imports or Arab oil, and he admitted he would exempt housing prices.
"So what's he going to freeze?", Mr. Trudeau shouted. "Your wages. He's going to freeze your wages."
So here the Prime Minister is talking about a program that is very similar to the program that he announced to the nation on Thanksgiving evening, a program that in essence will freeze the wages of working people. As I have said, it is very difficult to control professional fees and salaries, or profits and prices, or dividends and other forms of investment income. Suddenly there has been a turnabout. A government that was elected primarily because it was fighting against this type of program has now brought in a program of wage controls and so-called controls on

December 1, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
prices in Canada. I do not think it is the sort of program that we on this side of the House should let the government get away with.
Experience of this type of program in other parts of the world shows almost every time that wages have been controlled much more effectively than prices. Take the United States, for example. In August, 1971, wage increases in the United States averaged 13.5 per cent across the board. At the end of 1972, wage increases had fallen to 6.4 per cent. There was very effective wage control in the United States. In 1971, wages as a percentage of national income in the United States were 74.5 per cent. In 1975, they had dropped to 72.5 per cent. Once again this illustrates that the controls program brought in by President Nixon was very effective in controlling salaries, the wages of railway workers and other workers in the United States. At the same time, the percentage of national income going to big business went up from 14.6 per cent to 16.2 per cent, once again illustrating that controls on professional incomes and the incomes of the wealthy from dividends, profits, and so on, are by no means so effective as controls on the wages of ordinary people.
There is no rigidly defined method of controlling prices set out in this bill. The regulations will not be published until the bill passes parliament, so we do not know whether the government is really serious about controlling prices. Even if we had prior notification of price increases, once again there are all kinds of problems that are very difficult to solve. For example, in Britain there was a controls program in effect from 1968, to 1970 which required prior notification to their prices board of any price increases. But this did not work. It was terribly impractical.
In Britain the government estimated there were some some three million price changes per year in the period when these price controls were in effect, and over this three-year period there were only 2,162 prior notifications. Out of that number, only 345 were rejected. In percentage terms, only 0.0004 per cent of the price changes in Great Britain were actually held back by the board or changed by the board. This demonstrates it is very difficult to control prices in Canada, whereas it is very easy to control salaries and wages. The real victims of legislation of this sort will not be people who are unionized, but those who do not have a trade union to speak and fight for them when it comes to bargaining for a salary increase.
We have already seen examples in Canada of employers in certain corporations using the guidelines as an excuse for not raising the salaries of the people who work for them above the 8 per cent or 10 per cent level outlined by the guidelines, in spite of the fact that there are exceptions in the guidelines for some working people. I think that is one of the very unfortunate aspects of the bill before us. If I were an employer, I suppose my natural tendency would be the same; that is to say, this is a good reason for not giving my workers an increase in pay. I do not think this is fair and I think it will aggravate even more the disparity in wages and salaries in this country.
Another thing that really concerns me about this bill is the immense power it gives to the anti-inflation board. It 
gives the members of that board the power to interpret whether a certain cost that goes into the increased price is legitimate. It gives the members of that board the power to make decisions as to whether prices can be held back and what a fair profit is going to be. In other words, it gives the board a tremendous amount of subjective power interpretive in making judgments as to whether to be tough on certain corporations. When that type of power is given to any board, I automatically look to see who makes up the board, what type of people are to hold this power. I ask myself if they are likely to be fair, and is the membership a good balance of the Canadian people, the business community, the senior citizens, farmers and all Canadians? Is it a good cross-section of the people?
In this regard I find that the people on the board, as the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) has suggested, are really "poor" Canadians. They are people who have been involved in the business community as directors of huge corporations. They are people who do not really have any understanding of what it is like to live on a low salary in this country. These people will, naturally, have a certain bias in their approach and they will interpret these guidelines to reflect this bias.
I think the board would be much more effective, and fairer, if its membership reflected more what Canada is really all about. I want to spend a few minutes this afternoon putting on the record some of the background of the people sitting on the anti-inflation board. This is only a very brief sketch or summary of the background of some of them, but these people will have a tremendous impact on the people of my riding and on Canadians right across this country so I think it is only fair to examine the background from which they come.
First there is Jean-Luc Pepin, chairman of the board. If you examine the background of Mr. Pepin, you will find he has recently been the director of six companies in this country. He has been a director of the Power Corporation of Canada, Limited.

speechtext: And a university professor.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
He has been a director of the Canada Steamship Line, Celanese Canada Ltd., Collins Radio Co. of Canada Ltd., Westinghouse Canada Ltd., and Bombardier Ltd. These are corporations in which Mr. Pepin, the chairman of the anti-inflation board, has served as director.
Incidentally, the Power Corporation, which is the largest Canadian corporate conglomerate, seems to have certain ties with the Liberal party. I notice that between 1968 and 1972, for example-it is probably just coincidental that Mr. Pepin was minister of industry, trade and commerce at the time-this powerful corporation received $10 million in federal grants. Here we have Mr. Pepin, with this kind of business contact in his background, as chairman of the board, expected to make decisions that will provide a balance between contolling profits on one hand and the wages and salaries of workers on the other. I noticed the other day that Mr. Pepin's salary will be $54,000.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
No, $40,000.
December 1, 1975

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mrs. Plumptre will be getting $40,000, but Mr. Pepin will be getting $54,000 to head up this anti-inflation board. He will be the person telling many people earning $7,000, $8,000, $9,000, $10,000, $11,000, $12,000 and $13,000 to tighten their belts and restrain themselves. After all, Mr. Pepin took a great cut in salary as well. In order to take over the chairmanship of this board, he had to resign his corporate directorships and give up any revenue or income he might get from them. He had to give up his pension as a federal MP and cabinet minister. He can no longer make speeches and charge a fee or stipend for that. He himself said he had to make a sacrifice in only getting $54,000, and it is only fair that the people do the same thing. What hypocrisy!
Things like this make it difficult for the ordinary Canadian, the little guy, to accept seriously the idea that the government wants them to tighten their belts and restrain their attempts to obtain larger incomes for themselves. Mr. Pepin is not the only one on the board who has very strong background connections with the business community. Let us consider the so-called labour representative on this anti-inflation board. That is William Ladyman, a former vice-president of the CLC and also a retired member of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. This is the man the government has put on as the representative of labour, the working people of this country.
I find when I look into this man's background that he has had a couple of feet going in opposite directions. For example, in 1966 he became a director of the Polymer Corporation, thus putting one foot in the corporate door. Since then he has put his other foot in by becoming a consultant to the Great West Life Assurance Company. He has also been involved in several other endeavours that are clearly on the side of the corporate or business community. This is a man who does not in any way represent the labour interests of this country.
Then there is Jack Biddell and Harold Renouf. Renouf is a past governor of the Canadian Tax Foundation as well as a director of Associated Accounting Films International, based in New York. Mr. Biddell is president of Clarkson Gordon Ltd., an accounting firm. Earlier this year he made the statement that the government should encourage company and regional unions. Again, I think we have someone here who has a clear bias on the side of corporations and business.
As the remaining members of the board we have Claude Castonguay who has been a very prominent member of Mr. Bourassa's cabinet in Quebec. After he left provincial politics he, too, re-entered the business community as a corporate consultant and picked up a directorship in IMASCO Ltd. Then we have dear old Beryl Plumptre, the former chairman of the Food Prices Review Board. Again, her bias is very clear. She was chairman of the Food Prices Review Board in this country for a long while, but failed to find any excessive profiteering in the food industry. She was able to state that increases in the wages of the working people were primarily responsible for inflation in this country. She also said that marketing boards and government agencies which represent farmers were responsible for inflation.
Anti-Inflation Act
These people have a clear bias. This board is not balanced at all. It has a clear bias on the side of big business and corporations and I would be very surprised, indeed shocked, if the people on the board in any way tried seriously to control profits and prices in this country. They believe in the free enterprise method. They believe that the making of big profits is a really good thing. They believe that the bigger the profits, the bigger the reinvestment in the economy and the better the economy; that somehow the benefits will trickle down to the people at the bottom. This is the bias they have and I do not blame them for it. If you are to set up an anti-inflation program in this country and have a board to administer the program, surely the membership of that board should reflect all aspects of the Canadian economy. If that were the case, you would not have a single member now on the board representing the same point of view and probably supported by the Liberal party in this country.
Let us look at some of the loopholes in this bill on the price side. There are many loopholes to which no answers have been supplied by members on the opposite side. First of all, price increases will be accepted in general if the cost of producing the product goes up. How do you determine whether these are legitimate costs that are pushing up the prices of products to new levels? How do you police the transactions which go on within a corporation? How do you police what one arm of a corporation may sell to another arm of the same corporation? How do you police Bell Telephone when it deals with some of its subsidiaries?
These are questions which were not adequately answered in the committee. The only answer was that the board will have to make decisions, that it will have to use its best judgment. That is the reason I am concerned about the people on the board. If the board were more reflective of different thoughts, different people and different groups in this country, perhaps we could have a balanced interpretation of the law in respect of this program regarding which we have asked questions. But when all the people have a bias toward corporations, when between them they share many corporate directorships, I am certain the board will reflect that bias when making decisions of this sort.
How will they, for example, deal with the question of foreign ownership? How will they know whether or not a Canadian subsidiary is paying a fair price for something it purchases from its parent in the United States or some other country? How will they do that? Once again they will have to make a decision on the best information they have. I am sure their decision will reflect their bias. Once again may I say that if we had better representation on the board, I would be much more confident concerning the decisions made.
As if that is not enough, there are two exclusions written into the bill. A corporation will be exempt if it has an unusual productivity gain. What is an unusual productivity gain? How does one define that? I am sure the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) would define it in a different way than the chairman of the anti-inflation board, Jean-Luc Pepin. There is another exemption for an unanticipated cost development or cost benefit. What the devil is that? What is an unanticipated cost benefit or cost development? Maybe we should hire a psychiatrist or a

December 1, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
psychologist to sit on the board so that he can go to all these companies, such as the Power Corporation, Safe-ways, Loblaws, General Motors or any similar company to determine whether or not their cost benefit was unanticipated. We could have a lot of fun with that.
Once again, we have a board with the people on it now making that decision, and I am sure their definition of unanticipated cost benefit would be different from that of someone representing the working people, the farmers, or someone with a different point of view concerning how the economy should be run. These loopholes in the bill cause me to have a sense of lack of confidence in the government and in the program which has been brought before the House.
Then there are other inequities. We have the half-hearted attempt to control the fees of professional people. It seems to me the only way we can control the incomes of professional people is to tax back at a rate of 100 per cent anything over the maximum increase of $2,400. Many people in this House-including the minister, I believe- have stated that when you control the fees of professional people such as lawyers and doctors, they can get around that by seeing more clients or patients or, in the case of lawyers, by seeing more expensive clients. Even though their fees are frozen, their incomes can still go up by well over $2,400.
There are many dangers involved. In the case of medicine, for instance, the doctor could see his patients for a shorter period of time than usual and therefore perhaps see more patients a day. There is the possibility that the quality of health care in this country could decrease. There is also the hypocrisy and irony of allowing professional people to go above the so-called ceiling of $2,400 a year while working people and ordinary people must remain within the guidelines. If this program is to work, that part of it must be enforced. The government must be prepared to tax back at the 100 per cent rate any income above $2,400. If it is not prepared to do that, why in the devil is there this ceiling of $2,400 in the first place? Either the government is serious about this or it is not. If that is not done, this will be another part of the program which will turn out to be a farce.
Another thing which concerns me is that this year-we have heard very little debate about this-we are holding International Women's Year. Supposedly, as a country, we are trying to remove some of the inequities between men and women when it comes to salaries, working conditions and general treatment right across the country. Any bill that in essence will freeze or control salaries at a certain percentage will widen the inequity. If there is to be a salary increase of 10 per cent, this really means there will be more for someone making a bit more than there would be for someone at the lower end of the salary range.
We know that in general women receive less wages and are paid lower salaries than men. This type of program will freeze that inequity into the law for more years than might have been necessary. Indeed, it will widen the gap in salaries between men and women in Canada. I think in the past year or so there has been an attempt by some employers in this country to narrow the gap between women and men in terms of salaries. If we look at the guidelines which have been brought down, this type of attempt may not be

justified or allowed by the anti-inflation board if the increase in the salary of women happens to be above the guidelines laid down.
Another thing that concerns me in the guidelines, because the bill does not really say anything at all except mention the power to control salaries, prices and so on, is that dividends probably will not, in effect, be controlled as rigidly as salaries. Many people have pointed out that dividends will be frozen and have asked what the poor investor will do. I do not think that argument has much credibility. Dividends can be withheld by companies; they can be held back until after the program expires. Also, dividends could be plowed back into the corporation, thus increasing the value of the stocks, bonds or shares of the corporation. Once this program has been terminated, someone could cash in the bonds, stocks or shares and reap a capital gain. That is one way to get around it. Again, that is not fair. It is the person who has the money to invest who will not be affected as greatly as the janitor in your constituency, Mr. Speaker, or the CPR worker in my constituency.
Another thing in respect of this bill which I believe to be hypocritical is that before the bill was brought in, before the Prime Minister's announcement to the cabinet and immediately prior to the Thanksgiving night announcement, senior civil servants, senior executives and deputy ministers in this country received very large salary increases. Some of those increases were over $6,000 a year, on the very eve of the government saying to ordinary Canadians that they should tighten their belts and we must all make sacrifices and restrain ourselves, otherwise there will be real problems in respect of the economy.
Some of the civil servants who were involved in drafting these regulations and the bill received very large salary increases. When that happens, I believe it is very difficult for the ordinary Canadian to take the government very seriously. I think the goal of the government should be to redistribute income in this country and redistribute wealth. The bill before us today will not do that. In essence it will freeze some of the inequities we already have in the economy.
Another concern I have, which I should like to mention briefly, is in respect of government spending. I think all of us in this House would agree there is waste in government, that the government's spending in many areas could be cut back. The right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker) today mentioned that the Prime Minister's office had paid for a very expensive Christmas tree. Then there was the example of the swimming pool and other such waste. Surely many, if not all, of these things could be cut out. There are extravagant contracts which could be cut back. Information Canada and such agencies certainly could be cut back.
I want to say, however, that there are many social programs which should not be cut back. Many of them in Canada should be expanded. These are things the government will have to be very careful about in controlling inflation. Our party has said a number of time that the best way to control inflation in this country is to control the prices of the commodities we produce. Commodities such as oil are already controlled. Let us expand the two-price system to other commodities such as iron ore, nickel and
December 1, 1975

timber. This would be one way of bringing down the inflation rate in Canada.
Another way would be to control interest rates, control financial institutions and control mortgages in Canada. Another thing that could be done would be to control the price of energy. Also, we could do certain things in the area of food, that commodity being one of the greatest targets of inflation. If you had orderly marketing and price guarantees for farmers, there would not be the constant pressure on the price of food in Canada. These are things that could be done and our party has spoken about them often.
I want to say, in closing, that the government will not see its program succeed unless it makes radical changes to it, because in order to succeed the program must have the co-operation of all Canadians. In fact, most Canadians are probably very skeptical of the program. Two of the major parties have spoken against it and the labour movement is opposed to the program, as are many provinces who are asking questions about it. Unless changes are made, the program will not work. Certainly our party cannot support it on third reading.

It has the right of access and to share in the offices of any union.
Look at the powers that are incorporated in this bill. Are they subject to review by this House? No. Orders in council will have to be passed and, when passed, will be subject to examination by the committee on statutory instruments. However, that committee cannot reject any order in council that is passed according to the terms of legislation. It imposes guidelines on municipalities, crown corporations and otherwise, but not for the Government of Canada.
My colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), introduced an amendment to limit the government to its own stated guidelines and the declarations of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien). The government of course defeated that. It said it was unacceptable, impossible to follow or even accept.
Basically a program of controls is a very useful tool for fighting inflation as we know it today. The more I sit in this House the more I am amazed at the cabinet coming before this House asking for more and more powers. If they are not powers for the cabinet, they are powers for a bureaucracy. In many instances it has reached the point where this House is nothing but a pale and weak rubber stamp. Somehow or other, such is the feeling.
Government members feel they must support government. They feel they must support cabinet. Their reaction is supine. They act like jellyfish. They are wet noodles. I am talking very seriously to government members as well as to my own colleagues who often are quite prepared to accept this-the motto may be efficiency. However, in the name of efficiency more than one bootheel has been put on the neck of the citizenry. There is administrative efficiency, a close cousin to convenience.

We are dribbling out our birthright. Sometimes this is by handfuls. At other times, it is as thin as a slice of salami. But forever it is going out.
