Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to you for allowing me to address this honourable assembly on such an important issue as Bill C-73.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, this legislation deals with the controls of prices and wages. It was introduced after .due consideration because of the risks the Canadian economy would be running if no immediate remedy were found for this situation. This policy affects everybody: workers, employers, small businessmen and consumers alike. As a rule, a government policy affects only a very limited sector of our people; on the contrary, a legislation such as this affects most everybody. The decision of this government is the logical conclusion to a great many investigations and studies on the possible and likely consequences of this long and short term spiralling inflation on Canada.
The government is aware that such a price and wage control legislation will leave nobody indifferent. Yet, in spite of everything, the government had to take action and is taking action. Its action is centered on a policy called price and wage control, not price and wage freeze but price and wage control. As far as I am concerned, I admit that I have another expression in mind, namely the wage control and price freeze policy. Later on I will tell hon. members why I prefer and even recommend this expression. For the moment, let me single out some of the reasons which have forced the government to put such a legislation before the House. During last year, inflationary thrusts have scored in the vicinity of 11 per cent, and the forecasts were probably ranging between 15 to 18 per cent.
Anti-Inflation Act
Those forecasts were rather accurate when referring to the 71 per cent wage increase claimed by the postal worker union, the 45 per cent wage increase claimed by the Ontario teachers, and the same could be said for each one of the next collective agreements. Are those workers to blame who were claiming such high wage increases? I do not think so. Workers were trying to protect themselves against the unknown rate at which inflation could have got. Thus began the inflationary psychosis era. Indeed, the union leader were trying to get wage increases which would make up for very high inflationary thrusts. At the same time, companies drew up new price lists with the worst in mind, and raised prices accordingly. The eternal wheel which was spinning its way towards disaster and the inflationary expectations which had got hold of everybody appeared to be one of the major causes of inflation. I remember two or two and a half years ago, when prices were just beginning to rise more sharply, people were very much affected by each rise. Let us take for example the price of milk which rose by about 5 cents a quart. There was a wave of protest among consumers at that time. And the newspapers seized the opportunity to denounce the increase and predict a national disaster. At the same time, the price of a loaf of bread rose by 3 or 4 cents. Again people were indignant. Since then, the wheel of price increases has spun a great deal, because the problem is now worldwide.
There is a strange phenomenon which arises from this worldwide problem. People are so used to hear about wage increases and price increases all the time that they have resigned themselves to inflationary increases, and I would even say that they accept them. And it is precisely this acceptance which I call inflationary expectations. As proof of this for about six months, prices have risen staggeringly, but people no longer argue; they know what the cause is: inflation. And it is precisely this attitude that makes the lack of price controls extremely dangerous because businesses can raise their prices even inconsistently without any objection from the consumers who are paying.
In analysing those statistics, one also notes another very serious factor. Last year, indeed, wage increases in Canada reached 18 per cent. For the same period, they reached 9 per cent in the United States, and 8 per cent in Germany.
It must also be kept in mind that the United States make up 70 per cent of our import and export trade. Was it known that Canada won a silver medal last year? And, mind you, it was not at the Olympics. Indeed, Canada run second for the largest number of strikes to its credit. That world competition was won by Italy by the way. I think those facts are extremely important, all the more as we, Canadians, believe that we are among the best workers in the world, particularly among the most productive. Yet, when one considers the fantastic number of man-hours lost in this country, one realizes that the time has come to ask serious questions. Besides, one of the main causes of inflation in Canada is precisely the lack of productivity.
Several unions are now trying to demonstrate that salary increases are not a cause of inflation. They should indeed be more responsible than that and understand that salary increases are an integral part of the causes of such inflation. They are certainly not the only ones, of course.

December 1, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
The increased cost of raw materials, increased administrative costs, the lack of productivity and many other factors are also part of it. However, the responsibility or the role of salary increases should not be minimized. When it is known that in service industries 70 per cent of the expenditures incurred represent salaries, this means that every 10 per cent salary increase results in a 7 per cent increase in service costs. So, one must really be blind to suggest that salary increases in Canada are in no way a cause of the inflation facing this country.
I will now deal with the matter I raised at the outset, the reason of my preference for the title "Wage control and profit freeze" rather than "Price and wage controls". I mentioned "wage control" because the government allows salary increases up to 12 per cent, or a maximum of $2,400 a year. Which is not a freeze but a control that I find reasonable. As to companies with 500 employees or more, or 20 employees or more in the case of building industries, we are dealing not with profit control but actually with a profit freeze. In fact, the anti-inflation act allows no increase in profits for those companies. The only thing they are allowed to do is to raise their prices by an amount equal to their cost increases, which is to say that they are not allowed to increase their benefits.
I shall explain the consequences of the measure by giving you a simple example. A manufacturer produces shoes at a cost of $10 a pair, and sells them at a 20 per cent profit, that is to say for $12. Let us exaggerate a bit, to make the example that much more striking, and assume that production costs increase from $10 to $12. Without the anti-inflation act, the company, keeping a 20 per cent profit margin, would then sell those shoes for $24. However, because of the new act, the company will be entitled to a gross profit, not of $4 per unit but of $2, as was the case when its shoes cost $10 to produce. You will note, through that example, that profits are in fact being frozen and not controlled. On the other hand, the fact must be accepted that all companies will not come under this act.
As a matter of fact, as I said earlier, only the firms which have more than 500 employees on their payroll are included in this legislation. Therefore a certain number of firms could increase their prices beyond the standards set by Bill C-73. However, it should be noted that in this legislation there is one clause which gives the Anti-Inflation Board the power to order that some firms with fewer than 500 employees can become subject to this legislation. Why then did the government specify in the legislation that it included only the firms with more than 500 employees? The fact is that 60 per cent of Canadian productivity derives directly from these firms. Moreover, it is extremely easy for the board to control these companies, and this with a minimum staff because these large corporations have a very efficient accounting system.
This system is adequate, not to meet the needs of the government or of the Minister of National Revenue but to protect the shareholders. In these companies headed by a board of directors, the directors are elected for one year. If they did not have very adequate control or accounting systems, it would become easy for these directors to defraud the real owners, namely the shareholders. Most of those companies also have cost price systems. The executives know the exact cost of each item they produce or the

total cost for a group of items. These are the reasons for my saying that the Anti-Inflation Board will be able to control corporate prices in a very efficient manner and with a small staff. That is why I am not afraid to tell those who try to imply that such measures will be inefficient that they deceive people for egoistical purposes. It is precisely to allow the government to make an efficient control that the companies with fewer than 500 employees were excluded.
Several union leaders say that the import prices, which represent 30 per cent of the expenditures of Canadians, will not go down. On that point, I agree with them to some extent. Indeed, if U.S. inflation goes on eroding their economy, certainly the price of their products will go up proportionally and Canada will feel that increase. Yet, let us not forget that last year, wage increases in the United States were only 9 per cent, while in Canada they amounted to 18 per cent, as I said earlier. This means that the price of products imported from our neighbours will be lower. And even if the increases were higher than expected, Canadian industries and labour will benefit, because those products will be manufactured right here in Canada, instead of our having to import them and I am sure this would substantially contribute to the elimination of unemployment.
Last fall, I was delegated to the NATO economic commission. The representatives from the Federal Republic of Germany told us that one of the reason they had a low inflation rate was their labour union system. Indeed Germany has only one union per industry. If we had the same system here, there would be only one postal workers' union, one for Air Canada and so forth. This would result in an overall improvement of our economy, I am sure of that. Let me elaborate a little. Let us consider the mess due to our labour unions. When the letter carriers are on strike, mail sorters cannot work and moreover all Canadians must contribute to paying them unemployment benefits. The postmen's strike is over and now the inside workers are settling their collective agreement. They are also on strike and what is more ridiculous, as the postmen are unable to work, they are entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. This is why a single union in each economic sector would probably eliminate from 50 to 60 per cent of our strikes.
I will make a second suggestion, Mr. Speaker. When a strike is considered in any kind of private or public undertaking, a secret vote should be compulsory. I think that we are well aware of the unorthodox procedures used to compel people to vote according to the whim of union leaders.
In addition, the Department of Labour should control the counting of the secret vote, to make sure that the results are true by appointing employees to see that every operation is carried out according to law and order. I think that such procedure would liberalize the union movement, because I feel that a vote by a show of hands is anti-democratic and often removes individual freedom.
The government should also prescribe standard forms of financial reports to Canadian labour organizations. Indeed, acts passed by Parliament gave unions some taxation
December 1, 1975

power, which means that all employees of one company, whether they are willing or not, are imposed union dues which are levied at the source, from their pay, in exactly the same way provincial or federal taxes are collected.
When municipalities were given the power to tax, many requirements were included allowing constituents to be informed of how much was spent and where their money went. On the other hand, unions were invested with taxation power without any obligation to account in detail for their expenditure. Consequently, we can see under the heading "other", expenses of $2 million, $3 million or even $4 million in financial reports of Canadian unions. Do you not think that unions members who mandatorily pay their dues are entitled to ask for clear and precise financial reports and judge whether those expenditure are allowed for their own needs? In brief, how do union leaders administer these funds?
To conclude, I would like to draw the attention of all to a very important point. Even though this anti-inflation law is about to be passed and the majority of the business concerns will comply with it, yet we must not delude ourselves. Some concerns will try to get around it, in addition to all those with fewer than 500 employees which do not come under this law. For this reason, it is our responsibility to see that these concerns control their profits in a reasonable way.
Therefore, I ask people not to buy the products whose price is exorbitant, and to inform the Anti-Inflation Board. We .may be sure that those who manufacture those products will get the message quickly.
Let us all work together and the results will be positive for the greatest benefit of all.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to intervene in this debate in the House on Bill C-73 which, in my opinion and the opinion of my party, is one of the most powerful pieces of legislation that has ever been introduced. Perhaps second only to the Emergency Measures Act introduced, I believe, during World War I.
At the outset let me say I feel at this time in the debate, as we are drawing to the close of third reading, it is rather unfair, to say the least, of the government to expect us in opposition to, shall I say, buy a pig in a poke. We have a bill which in one respect gives the Anti-Inflation Board extreme powers in a democracy. There are no regulations as yet. Nothing has been firmed up, but the government is saying we should pass the bill and then it will give us the regulations.
My party wishes to continue this debate as long as we can to show the people of Canada that we as a democratic party, and I think I speak for many members on this side, are not prepared to give the government carte blanche without having some assurance that the board itself will be restrained in its use of the dictatorial powers being given in this bill. I think this is one of the most important aspects of this debate.
Government members for obvious reasons are attempting to play down the tremendous power given in this bill. Another reason why we oppose the bill, and there are several, is not an opposition to the fight against inflation,
Anti-Inflation Act
but an opposition to the unfairness of this piece of legislation. It is unfair because the axe does not fall evenly on all sectors of the economy or the working force.
No one is going to convince me that a lawyer, and I am not blaming all lawyers, cannot increase his income next year by 20 per cent or 25 per cent as a result of this bill. The bill includes a productivity clause, and if a lawyer wants to take on more clients or wealthier clients, or gets involved in a $400,000 or $500,000 real estate deal, his income will go up by more than $2,400, without even considering the fee schedule.
I am not saying all lawyers are going to take advantage of this clause, or that all doctors are going to do likewise. I am saying that these people can increase their incomes above the stated amount. Certainly lawyers can in the way I have mentioned, instead of piddling around with $30,000 mortgages. As far as I can determine most doctors are over-worked now. Supposing a doctor does have five patient consulations an hour instead of three, that represents a very significant increase in income.
This is the kind of thing that those on fixed incomes, or those who belong to the trade union movement, or teachers' associations resent. The teachers were here on the Hill today and I spoke to them out front, as did the minister. I congratulate him for having the courage to go out there and face them. They were very militant, and I do not think he had very much to say. But this is the kind of thing that really galls these people because they know any increase they will get will specifically be 8 per cent, plus 2 per cent, plus another possible 2 per cent. What they do not know is how this board, with no regulations so far, is going to govern prices and profits. As long as this doubt remains these people will become more infuriated as the months go by and as we see that prices are not kept in line with wages and salaries.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) may think he has seen some opposition to this bill so far. If it does not work I suggest that he will see a great deal more opposition. I suggest that the bill is not going to work in its entirety, and not even in part. The real trouble will come next spring or summer when people have been required to hold back on wages and salaries but they see prices continuing to rise.
A perfect example of this is the increase in food prices since October 14. Let no one be fooled by this tremendous generosity on the part of four, five, or six major food chains in the country, and I would put "tremendous generosity" in quotation marks. These major food chains have already raised their prices in the last six weeks, and they have already bargained with the processors and distributors so they know they can go easy for 60 days. They are not going to lose any money, and the average consumer is not going to be taken in. Consumers see through this.
Average people are not angry enough yet as the full effects of this powerful, authoritarian piece of legislation have not been felt. But when that occurs, probably in six to eight months, we will see tremendous social discord. We will have groups fighting other groups. This bill will be divisive rather than a bill to bring people together.
Members opposite suggest it is unpatriotic to oppose the bill or not go along with the legislation. I suggest at this

December 1, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
time it is the government that is being unpatriotic by forcing various groups to fight other groups. Just this afternoon in the Citizen one newspaperman wrote about planned economic changes. I am not suggesting these have been endorsed by the cabinet, but this is the kind of government restraint we are to see. Governments are among the biggest spenders. What are the cuts they intend to make? Apparently we are going to see three day a week mail delivery. That is one suggestion. There is the elimination of LIP, OFY, CYC, and the phase-out of the science department as well as the end of Information Canada. I do not think that would be a bad move, although it would eliminate some jobs. Then there is the freeze on research spending.
I have heard members from other parties say that the government should trim the fat. People have said it is the fault of the government, and that we must cut down on government spending. This is very dangerous because when we wipe out OFY, LIP, CYC, the science department and so on, this means we are cutting out jobs. If we cut out these jobs what will happen? Is it better to see that these people are employed at a meaningful job so that they will pay taxes, or is it better to lay them off? If they are laid off the chances are that they will not go to private industry, because when there are already 720,000 people out of work the only route they have to follow is through the UIC or through welfare when the unemployment insurance runs out.
If the government is to trim its costs obviously it cannot trim its transfer payments and socially-oriented programs. It must create jobs and good social services. Are we to negate all the best legislation that has been passed in the last ten years and wipe it out because we must trim federal spending? As other members of my party have already stated, the fundamental question concerning this program is whether we have a just approach to dealing with inflation, or an incomes policy. I suggest the two are separated here. Having studied the white paper and the bill, the answer is that the approach the government has adopted is unfair and unworkable. We in this party cannot accept it in any way, shape or form. A few moments ago I alluded to the teachers from Toronto who were demonstrating on the Hill this afternoon.

Also when the teachers in the city of Toronto compare what they have been offered by their board, which the Anti-Inflation Board has knocked down, with what the same teachers make in the city of Ottawa or in Windsor,

they say they are all teachers and that they have all put in at least four years at university. In fact this is one of the most highly educated professions in the country as a whole. It is this kind of unfairness or lack of justice that will badly divide this country. How do I know? It has already happened. I just gave an example. It has brought bitterness to one group of teachers, the teachers in the city of Toronto, because it is unfair. I think we have already proven before the first regulation is brought in that this legislation is unworkable.
It is becoming increasingly evident as time passes that the government in its attempt to secure a lower rate of price inflation has adopted a policy of wage restraint to deal with the matter. In other words, the burden of this program is being placed on the wage earners of the country, particularly the low wage earners. There is no doubt about that. I do not know how anyone who has finished high school, has gone through university, and is now earning $7,800 in the city of Toronto-I admit this is the low end of the scale-can live. I do not know how they can live on $7,800 in the city of Brantford, from where I come.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before I called it 6.30 p.m. I was concentrating on the divisive aspects of this bill which pits groups against groups, unions against unions, organizations against organizations, and businessmen against businessmen.
I could give you the example of a small company settling a wage contract of, say, 18 per cent or 20 per cent a week before the anti-inflation bill becomes law, and a similar corporation making the same product being held to the 10 per cent guideline. You can rest assured that the small companies particularly will be fighting it out with the Anti-Inflation Board because one company might have to pay higher labour costs while competing in the same market with another company which does not have to pay those higher costs. As I said earlier, this is an infamous, authoritarian bill which gives the government powers that should not be given to any government in a democracy such as ours.
I would like now to dwell for a few moments on our export situation. I think this is one of the major thrusts of the government's arguments in favour of Bill C-73. I would like to begin by simply asking: are we to accept the statements of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) that Canada's international competitive position and ability to pay its own way in the world are being set back because of our current wage trends?
Statistics Canada reported that on a year to year basis the rate of increase for imported goods was 14.5 per cent and only 7.5 per cent for exported goods. Furthermore, just a few days ago, some five weeks after the introduction of wage and price guidelines, trade figures issued by Statistics Canada showed that sales of finished goods rose 9 per cent in the first ten months of 1975. Thus, despite gloomy warnings that Canada is losing its edge in world markets, the best performance this year is coming from manufacturers. Statistics Canada reported also that exporters of finished goods are now doing better business and making greater inroads into foreign markets than they were last year when economic conditions were far more buoyant.
Based on the above it is no wonder that various groups have been less than exuberant over the ramifications of this program. As I have already said, this package of controls is nothing but wage restraints predicated on the phony assumption that wages have led the way in the inflation spiral.
As I said earlier this afternoon, it is always the low income earners who are blamed for overspending and for inflating the economy. But I wonder how often those in power on the treasury benches-I do not see many of them present-sit back and reflect on two points: one, if you are making $7,500 a year, how in heaven's name can you
Anti-Inflation Act
overspend? I do not know what the national average income is today; it is probably about $10,500 or $11,000. Even then, how can you overspend and create inflation on that? The other point is that these people are bombarded day in day out through the electronic media to buy, buy, and buy. It does not matter what the quality of the article is, what its workmanship is and whether or not you need the damn article-you are told to go out and buy it.
If there is anyone causing inflation in this country, or who has caused it in the last ten years, it is those people who have told everybody to go out and buy. They have psyched them to the point where they are almost reacting like Pavlov's dogs so that they have to go out and buy. But who is reaping the benefits from it? It creates employment, but we get back to the same point again that as it creates employment there are more people to spend money, and we are back in the vicious circle of inflation.
If the infamous Bill C-73 becomes law, who will get it on the head? The guy who has been told to buy, buy, buy. This is the ridiculous aspect of the economy of this country today. I deplore it and I deplore the fact, as I said earlier, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) refuses to take part in this debate, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said earlier today. He should take part in this debate and give us on this side of the House good reasons for voting for this bill, the regulations pertaining to which have not even been drawn up yet. We do not even know what we are voting for.
In the early stages of this debate some Canadians expressed a degree of satisfaction with the anti-inflation program. I suggest that the reason for this is that the major attraction of any income policy is that it promises-I stress the word promises-price controls as part of the package. But if the promise is a hollow promise and there is no real, effective legislation to back up that promise and to make sure that prices and profits are in fact controlled, then we descend into the area of cynicism, and if there is one thing this country can do without today it is cynicism. That is why I am opposed to this bill. It will create more cynicism. It will not reduce it.
This promise of price controls had to be introduced because the government realizes that wage earners will readily ease off from demanding higher incomes if they are assured that prices will be kept stable. This is a point we have stressed for years. Yet how does this policy operate with respect to prices? We now all know that the guidelines explicitly say that wages cannot rise beyond specific percentage points each year. There are no such specifics in regard to prices, and that, again is what creates cynicism and the divisiveness which will develop from this authoritarian piece of legislation.
Other members of my caucus have gone to great lengths to point out that price increases are taking place in three principal areas: food, shelter, and energy. In fact, of all the inflation we have in this country approximately 65 per cent is in the area of food, shelter, and energy, and it is in these three areas that the controls policy will have little or no effect. I think that is a very important point.
All hon. members of this House no doubt were inundated with calls to their homes and constituency offices regard-

ing the dramatic rise in the cost of food following the introduction of this program. After all, prices can increase to cover increased costs, whatever they might include. We still do not know what increased costs are all about. Only Jean-Luc Pepin knows. He claims he knows for sure. In terms of food costs, people just have to pray that their frozen wages will be enough to cover their increased costs. The advantage is clearly on the side of the corporations which know exactly what their wage costs will be. They can plan now. They know the limits. The limits are there, thanks to the Liberals, and thanks to the government.
I wish to make one last point regarding food costs. All of us have noticed the full page ads which major food chains have taken out since their announced 60 day price freeze on November 21.1 alluded to this earlier in my address late this afternoon. One such ad reads, and I quote, "Loblaws freezes prices." William Sherman, president of Loblaws, says in the ad that this action is being taken in, and I quote "recognition of the consumers' growing concern over food price inflation." I love that.
Before consumers embrace the Christmas good will of all the food chains, they should keep this in mind: as reported a few nights ago food chain spokesmen stated that, and I quote, "There is a standard industry practice involving private agreements between the stores and their suppliers." In other words, chains such as Loblaws will not have to absorb price increases until mid January because pre-bargaining with their suppliers will cost the food chains virtually nothing. William Sherman said, and I quote, "many suppliers have already taken their increases, and we requested that there be no increases during December." Big deal-60 days!

speechtext: That is the Christmas spirit.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Therefore the risk to chains such as Loblaws, Steinberg's and other major chains is minimal. What happens after 60 days? Can we count on good corporate gestures come January or February? I doubt it very much.
As I said this policy, and this program, do not apply to the key elements in the cost of living. Since wage bargaining takes place in the open, and since any increase is subject to stringent regulations, the government can make wage restraints stick. It is a very simple thing. We have heard that many times before in this House, and I do not hesitate for a moment to repeat it tonight. As long as we have the democratic right to keep talking against this bill, we on this side of the House will keep talking against it.
Price decisions, on the other hand, are not as easily identifiable. Here again my colleagues have cited numerous examples of the inability to pin down what constitutes increased costs. Thus far we have had no comprehensive statements on how costs will be monitored. The Federation of Independent Businessmen cited several examples of how large corporations can hide their profits. For example, General Motors in Canada sees that profits for the coming year will increase appreciably. The head office in the United States then proceeds to charge the Canadian subsidiary higher management fees. In effect, G.M. of Canada faces higher costs, and the consumer is left with having to pay those costs-not General Motors, but the people who buy G.M. cars.

The only impression with which consumers are left is that price controls are merely a symbolic gesture in the incomes policy. It is not extraordinary then that groups such as the CLC, QFL, the National Council of Welfare, and the anti-poverty organization, to name a few, have condemned this national belt tightening campaign. Prices in key elements of the economy will not even be touched, and this the government admits and has admitted.
Aside from food costs, which I have already mentioned, energy costs to the average consumer will be up this year. In fact they are going up right now. Because of the government's excise tax, it will cost more to drive. Because of the government's changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act, those on lower incomes will have to pay higher premiums proportionately. Because of the government's inaction in the housing industry, houses will not be available to most Canadians who are looking for housing this year.
In this program the average consumer is being told that it is he and his wages which have to be restrained. Workers are becoming increasingly disenchanted with what they see happening. The current rate of inflation in Canada is 11.3 per cent and, if this situation does not change, workers' real incomes will fall by about 1.3 per cent. Again, keep in mind that inflation in 65 per cent of a family's costs will not be controlled. I am talking about food, shelter, and those other basic commodities such as clothing and so on.
The Minister of Finance has made much of the fact that this policy is designed to benefit those worst off in society. Nothing, in my opinion, could be further from the truth. What this program does, by means of everyone being entitled to receive the same percentage increase, is to freeze the present situation. Granted, those on lower incomes are being given a measly $750, if they can get it. There is no guarantee. The folly of this was exemplified, as I said earlier this afternoon, by Quebec's actions, to which I referred earlier. The power to obtain any sizable increase- that is, to those on low or fixed incomes-rests with the provincial governments, and if one is treated in the fashion with which Quebec has treated its people, I suppose that is tough. I think this is an important point. I have not raised it before.
The Government of Canada could use this bill in a very effective way to begin to narrow the gap between the rich and the poor. If it wanted to use this bill, it could say, for example, that anyone earning less than $11,000 or $12,000 per year would be exempt from the guidelines. From there on the percentage increase in income would decline, so that by the time a person reaches $24,000 per year he receives no increase, regardless of productivity. However, the government will not use the bill in this way, and I suggest that the reason it will not is that it is still tied in with the old Manchester school, the old nineteenth century school. Economists of the nineteenth century thought there was no ceiling to an income one can earn, provided you scratched your way up over people's backs, even your mother's back. They thought the sky was the limit to incomes.
Where does that philosophy lead us? Look at the major cities of the United States, that great land of free enterprise, and their skyscrapers. My God, what has bigness
December 1, 1975

brought that country-nothing but misery, social distress, crime, hatred, bitterness, class against class, people against people, organization against organization. I suggest that this bill will help to contribute to that kind of social psychology in this country, and for that reason I oppose it.
There is no doubt in my mind that low-paid workers will not be better off under this program. On the other hand those on the other end of the scale will do very well. Dividends will not be controlled because companies will be able to increase dividend payments to obtain capital on the stock market. Furthermore, dividends will be paid out to the owners of corporations after this policy ends. In other words, dividend payments may be deferred. This suggests, Madam Speaker, that we shall witness in the next few years a redistribution of wealth, not from the rich to the poor, but in favour of the rich and powerful.
Probably the strongest condemnation of this type of program came from the Prime Minister himself, when he said about 18 months ago that you can't freeze executive salaries and dividends because there are too many loopholes to squeeze through. Meanwhile the Prime Minister has turned 180 degrees. Now he says we must have controls, although 18 months ago he was desperately courting votes with exactly the opposite policy. No wonder he will not enter the debate. He has not the nerve to come to this House and explain why he changed his mind. During the election the Prime Minister said that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), for whom I personally, and my party have a great deal of respect, would not freeze prices of farm produce. But this 1975 program will not do this either. The Prime Minister went on to say that prices of United States imports and of Arab oil would not be affected. I ask, what is left to control?

The government had to do something to prove that only it could provide the leadership this country needed, indeed has demanded for 18 months but has not received. As my colleague from Regina-Lake Centre said in a speech last week, many workers, union people included, voted for the government on the assumption they were voting against controls as advocated by the official opposition, those very same types of controls we face today.

much different because of the fact that the government is taking over control for 39 months. That is a long time for a government to take over economic control of a country. Just think of those people who have perhaps only ten years left in order to make their livelihood and provide for their retirement. Our inflationary factor today would be much worse if it were not for the fact that Canadians are a resourceful people. They are a great people. They are a strong people. It was suggested today, I believe by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, that we are second worst in the world so far as our destruction of our work ethic is concerned. This means there is dissatisfaction-a great deal of dissatisfaction-and we are therefore destroying the spirit that has built this country.
I have a great fear that this is what is going to happen unless there is a turn around, and it has to be in the very near future. I am not prepared to sell my birthright for a bowl of porridge, but unfortunately I am caught up in this process. Many people have said we should go along with this program because of the fact that the government hasn't got anything else. Well, that's a pretty lame excuse for supporting a program which you do not think is going to be in the best interest of a country, when there could be a better one put in its place. I want now to read just a few statements made by a gentleman who I think is going to become very well known to a great many Canadians, including the Minister of Finance. This is what he says: I read from the report before me.
Regulations to implement Ottawa's anti-inflation program will be "too restrictive and inflexible" for business, according to Toronto accountant J. L. Biddell.

The country must reach a consensus on the causes of inflation during the control period to prevent a return to an unacceptable period of rapid price escalation, he said.

We have to warn the Canadian people what they are about.
While approving the general intent of the government's program, my leader and other members of our party made it clear from the outset that we had grave reservations about some of the major features of Bill C-73, and that we would not commit ourselves as to our ultimate position on third and final reading until we saw what kind of amendments emerged from committee examination of the bill. We put forth our amendment, and I have explained the difference between our position and their position, and why this amendment was not passed.
It is of fundamental importance that Canadians should realize that what could be accomplished in 18 months should be all that is required in the best interests of the country. We are not taking anything away from the bill by this 18 months period. If at the end of that time it is found there have to be other controls put into place, I am sure members of the opposition would be ready to go along. If the government would like to bring in a different program we might be ready to agree to that also. However, as I say, we would like to restrict the program to 18 months, and we would like also to give the Anti-Inflation Board an opportunity to criticize the government for any failure on its part to follow the guidelines, just as it is able to criticize business and labour.

While we may not have agreed with all of their particular criticisms, the comments and statements of these groups have reinforced the view that the government program is, at very best, pretty rough justice, with a number of built-in inequities and distortions.

Rather, they indicate that the government is still very much feeling its way, unclear even in its own mind on many important aspects of the program, including the all important question of relationships with provincial governments. That is very important, Madam Speaker.
How in the world can a program work without the support of the provincial governments? Why was not support of all provinces asked for prior to embarking upon the program? The answer is simply that there was not time. The Prime Minister announced the program without communicating with the provincial premiers in advance. People will put up with this program for a short period of time, and we thought 90 days was the right period. But the minister says the period will be 39 months. This is why we have reservations about this bill. It is also causing concern among various business groups. It is a great misfortune, Madam Speaker, that our friends to our left are so far left that they cannot even understand the fact that the economy is better in private hands than in government control.
I have been contacted by some professional people who are concerned about the outcome of this legislation and what it will mean to them. This is why I say we are now getting to the stage where it is a matter of survival for certain segments of our economy. One of these groups has this to say:
We would like to take this opportunity of expressing our concerns in these matters in the hope that our representatives can make the government aware of them, before the regulations are finalized, as it will be difficult if not impossible to change the regulations after they become law.
Fundamental to applying price control regulations to auditing and accounting practices is an understanding of the good will factor inherent in many professional accounting practices in Canada today. Good will represents the intangible value of having an established clientele who continue to deal with the same firm. The value of good will however becomes tangible when an incoming partner pays hard cash for it. The purchaser has in effect purchased the right to a share of the income of the accounting practice. In an established practice the older partner anticipates that he will be able to sell his good will on retirement. Thus many practising professional accountants have spent many
December 1, 1975

years of their lives investing their time and ability in establishing a practice that will be saleable when they retire. This investment is analogous to the employer's contribution to a pension plan on behalf of an employee in that both have planned and look forward to these funds as part of their retirement income.
It is therefore imperative that the wage and price controls be administered fairly and great care must be taken to ensure that the value of good will is not impaired or destroyed. The impairment or destruction of good will would cause economic chaos to the accounting profession and would be the equivalent to imposing a 100 per cent capital tax.
They go on to say this:
We are aware of an accounting practice which has a July year end. At July 31, 1974 this was a four man practice and the practice income was shared four ways. On August 1, 1974 one of the partners retired and the three remaining partners purchased his partnership interest including good will and have contracted to pay him a capital payment for good will over a period of years. On July 31, 1975 the practice was a three man practice who now share the retired partner's income. Thus the remaining partners' incomes materially increased in 1975 and if the difference in incomes from 1974 to 1975 were confiscated by way of a tax the remaining partners would be unable to complete their obligations.
I am sure the minister gives cognizance to the fact that a lot of business people are caught up in this program. With the continued invasion of government into private affairs we have to rely more upon specialized professions to protect our personal well being. This group goes on to say:
When one considers the strenuous effort required to build and maintain a professional practice; the liability of the professions to the public and the fact that a professional has to provide for his own retirement are factors that should be considered before making hasty adjustments to the very roots of this type of business.
In conclusion, with respect to the effect on good will, we are concerned that there may be an unfair, and perhaps unintended, side effect of the legislation and regulation: it appears probable that they may result not only in a limitation on income but also have the effect of confiscating capital. This, we suggest, must be avoided if equity in the efforts to control inflation is to prevail.
So it is obvious there is great concern in the country about where we are going. After all, it takes all kinds of people to make our economy work, such as the professions, labour, and all segments of society. We must work together if our economy is to get ahead; we must get away from the kind of misunderstanding that has occurred under the present administration.
Given the degree of rough justice involved, given the economic distortions which are virtually inevitable in this kind of program, and given the well founded mistrust that we have for the government's motives and willingness to deal openly and frankly with the people of Canada, we are not prepared to hand the Prime Minister and his ministers these extraordinary powers without any effective time limit on their use.

Madam Speaker, the peanut gallery to our left is in fine form this evening. This is third reading of a bill which euphemistically is known as the Anti-Inflation Act, Bill C-73. It is a bill to deal with inflation.
This is an incredible development, coming about a year and a half after the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in co-operation with his cohorts to my left, stumped up and
Anti-Inflation Act
down the country saying that price and incomes controls are absolutely the worst thing that could ever be undertaken by a government in an attempt to fight inflation. Every possible adjective of condemnation was used to decry price and incomes controls to fight inflation. Yet 18 months later, on Thanksgiving Day last October 13, the Prime Minister sat down to a meal of crow and announced to the nation price and incomes controls.
This new example of leadership, it is said, will take us out of the economic morass in which we find ourselves. One wonders what occurred, what caused this transformation. What caused this proud government and its Prime Minister to eat crow on Thanksgiving Day? What caused it to do an 180 degree flip and advocate policies that it wasted no energy in condemning over a year previously? Was it a change in the economic situation? Was it the sudden realization that the economy was in bad shape, and suddenly inflation was perceived to be a serious problem? That is some change, but that is the essence of what the Prime Minister tried to convince the country. Yet an examination of the figures, the numbers, the indices, the measures of economic performance, inflation, and the consumer price index now indicate there was no dramatic change. They indicate there was no disastrous trend in the last two years, and no dramatic change suddenly before Thanksgiving Day to bring on this turn-around.
The second theory proposed by some political observers is that this was really a Machiavellian plot. The suggestion is that in fact the leading indicators showed that inflation was on the way down now and that the economy was due to improve, and the Machiavellian devil that he is, the Prime Minister, felt by introducing this program he could then claim credit for leadership. This has been proposed by a few media observers of the political scene in Canada. I tend to dismiss that because if that was the motivation behind the Thanksgiving announcement surely there would have been better preparation and a more complete program offered. Surely we would not have the uncertainty and the wishy-washy change in opinion and direction the government has demonstrated since.
The third reason proffered by some observers of the political scene for this about-face by the government has to do more with the state of the Liberal party than the state of the economy. The rationale behind this reasoning is that there has been a considerable amount of discontent since July, 1974. The energy, the new direction, and leadership expected by the Liberals after their victory were just not there, and by the summer of 1975 that discontent was starting to manifest itself in audible grumbling. The Prime Minister then chose to appoint an old friend to the communications portfolio rather than a sitting member, which gave rise to even more grumbling and discontent. Then the former minister of finance resigned, and the public outpouring of discontent became nearly deafening.
At this point it is suggested that Senator Keith Davey was able to convince the Prime Minister that prices and incomes controls would let the Prime Minister seize the reins of leadership again, demonstrating vigour and vitality in attacking problems of the economy, and this would in fact allow him to turn the situation around and pass the upcoming vote of confidence at the Liberal convention.

December 1, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
Quite frankly, that theory has a lot of credence, and is substantiated by a lot of observations for those who want to look at them. It is really tragic that the economic initiatives taken by the government should be dictated by considerations such as that rather than by the state of the economy. It is tragic that the Prime Minister would play games with the economic lives of millions of Canadians because he had to face that vote of confidence at the Liberal party convention.
Whatever reasons there were, on October 13, Thanksgiving Day, the Prime Minister said we were going to have a system of prices and incomes control. That was an infamous October 13. Fans of the now defunct comic strip character Pogo will recall that when Friday 13 fell on Monday one had great reason for concern. We now understand and see some wisdom in that comic book character's philosophy.
Flowing from that October 13 statement is the bill that is before us tonight, C-73, called in clause 1 the "Anti-Inflation Act". That in itself is reason enough to vote against the bill because there is nothing anti-inflationary about it. This is not an anti-inflation act. It is not an act to impose a system of wage and price controls. This act is nothing more than a means of giving sweeping and extraordinary powers to a so-called Anti-Inflation Board and an administrator still unnamed. That is all this bill does.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) spoke in general terms about the scope of the wage and price control program they had in mind for the country, but we do not know what it is. This House does not know what it is, and the country does not know what it is. I suspect that those on the other side, including the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, do not know what it is. I suspect they are still working on it.
This bill is not an anti-inflation program and not a wage and price controls program. We will not be voting on either of those things. A realistic anti-inflation program that addressed itself truly to the root causes of inflation would combine prices and incomes controls with other features. Prices and incomes controls by themselves without the other features in the program are worse than nothing at all. In a sense the Prime Minister was absolutely right last year during the election campaign when he said that price and income controls were bad. They are bad if that is the sum total of the anti-inflation program because by themselves they can do more harm than good. It is the steps the government must take during an anti-inflation program, while price and income controls are in place, that would constitute an anti-inflation program.
What are those opportunities or steps? One of them quite clearly has been referred to repeatedly, but apparently the lesson still remains to be learned by those on the other side. This step has to do with government spending and the money supply. I should like to quote from a report by Dr. Philip Cramm of Texas A & I University, reported in the February, 1975, issue of World Oil. Dr. Philip Cramm, to put this in context, is a consultant who has worked for the International Monetary Fund, the U.S. and the Canadian governments. He states:
-there has never been a prolonged general price inflation in recorded history that was not preceded by and directly related to a growth in money supply. In our economy a growth in money supply occurs

principally when the government spends more than it taxes and prints money to make up part of the deficit.
That is precisely what has been happening in Canada. Since 1968 when this administration took over spending has gone wild, up by some 300 per cent, with deficit followed by deficit. These deficits have been financed by the printing of money, that is, by the selling of bonds to the Bank of Canada which in turn prints the money to pay for the bonds.
In spite of the claims repeated so many times in the past that we are the victim of world circumstances and that world inflation is at the root of our problems, a fact echoed just recently this evening by members of the NDP, the bulk of inflation in this country is domestic, and one of the main causes is that our money supply has gone berserk to finance government spending, which has also gone berserk.
In addition to the question of money supply and proper management is the matter of the discipline the government exercises in respect of the money it spends. For the record I should like to quote from a policy review report in 1975 by the C. D. Howe Research Institute. This report states among other things:
It is clear that governments will have to impose a new form of spending discipline on themselves, because there are not sufficient natural restraints forcing them to assess the productivity of their spending. As a first step in this process of self-discipline, the public should be given more and better information on the spending process.
That is a polite non-partisan way of saying the government is spending our money in an unwise and inefficient fashion. In addition to the magnitude of the spending, this inefficient spending is one of the root causes of inflation.
This afternoon the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) gave numerous examples of the wasteful extravagance of government spending such as on the Prime Minister's residence, frills, tapestry, and all the [DOT]accoutrements of power-spending which certainly the average Canadian can hardly appreciate makes his life better.
I do not intend to dwell on this at any great length, but I want to refer to an article in this morning's Montreal Gazette by Don Sellar. He says that the contract given Mr. Roy MacLaren, a consultant whose Liberal party connections are well established and who was chairman of a 1974 fund-raising dinner for the Liberals, was that he would receive up to $158,000 in government money in return for his services in two years. This includes up to $20,000 a year in expense money, a daily allowance of up to $35 a day for food and accommodation while in Ottawa, and a special allowance of up to $4,000 a year for transportation to and from Toronto to visit his family. This gentleman was to get $158,000 of our money.
When the government spends its citizens' money in this fashion how can this have any effect other than to debase our currency and debase our taxes? The citizen does not consider, in this type of example, that taxes are his way of contributing to the financing of the operation of a government which performs services on his behalf. He looks at this sort of thing and says that the government is wasting his money. To him taxes represent something extracted
December 1, 1975

from him by law so that when he sends in a dollar from his salary he does not consider that 20 cents from it will go for housing, 30 cents for food, and so much for the salary of his member of parliament. He says that the government is ripping him off to satisfy its friends. So he will not be satisfied with an increase of $1 but will want an increase of $1.50. It is that sort of attitude toward government which is one of the root causes of inflation. This is the example this sort of thing sets for public servants and those in the private sector.
There was a time when public servants and members of the government viewed themselves as trustees of our money and acted accordingly. The example was set by government in that it had an obligation and responsibility to be frugal and efficient in the spending of our money. Frills were to be avoided in the way they would be avoided by any trustee if he is to have the respect of the individual whose funds he administers. That, however, seems to have gone by the board. Frills and wasteful spending are the norms for this government, and represent one of the root causes of inflation.
A third cause of inflation which must be addressed in any discussion of an anti-inflationary program is the matter of the position of the power groups in our society. This is a position about which John Crispo of Toronto has written and spoken. There exists in our society numerous groups which have grown up in the last few years which have the power to overcome the restraints which exist in a free enterprise system. These groups which we know as big business, big labour, and big government are immune to normal restraints. When there is an increase in wages they pass on the increase. When there is inflation they receive a larger share of the pie. An increase in taxes means nothing. Ironically the Minister of Finance alluded to that when he spoke on second reading on the bill when he said:
The goal of narrowing the gap in income distribution can be thwarted if those in higher brackets are successful in maintaining or increasing their own real, after tax, share of take-home pay by pushing up their income levels.
If instead of talking about those higher brackets he had in fact generalized about those in positions of power he would have been right on. But I do not see any evidence that the government appreciates that these power groups are able to misdirect the economy or that there is any willingness on their part to find some solution. With the powerful looking after themselves, it is the weak, the unorganized, who in fact are paying the price. That is what is happening.

If in fact the hon. member would applaud equally as loud when I say it is important to attack those power groups which are able to exert their influence over, the weak and the non-influential then I would be assured that his thought processes are straightened out.
We need evidence that the government is attacking the real causes of inflation before we or the Canadian public will be convinced that the government has a true antiinflation program. This bill is not an anti-inflation program. It is not even a price and income control program. It
Anti-Inflation Act
is nothing more than a bill to give some extra-ordinarily vast powers to an administrator and an anti-inflation board. Even if it were considered as part of an anti-inflation program it would still be subject to very serious criticism. For that reason it is impossible for us to support it.
The main benefits of price and income controls are the psychological benefits. They provide an example of the seriousness of the problem as viewed by the government. After the government spent many months condemning such a program it is small wonder the public is very skeptical about this program. They say the government tells them one thing and then turns around and does the opposite the next year.
Even as a psychological tool or as a strong medicine, as a few people have described it, it must be responsible. We must be very careful in terms of the powers granted by this bill. It is indeed strong medicine. Price and income controls represent strong medicine. When I refer to medicine we must remember that when we have strong medicine it should be administered in limited dosage. You do not call for the open ended, unlimited administration of strong medicine, which is essentially what this bill does. One observer likened controls to a narcotic. He said that your head tells you it is not good, but it seems almost irresistible and once on it, it is tough to get off. A narcotic is not a cure, it is simply a way to kill pain temporarily, but if you get on it and take it for too long, it becomes addictive and very difficult to get off it.
My friends to the left are wondering if we advocated narcotics. Let me continue with the medical analogy and tell you that there is a role for pain killers in medicine, and in fact as part of our anti-inflationary program with which we faced the Canadian people we stated in all honesty that price and income controls were part of an over-all package, necessary pain killing medicine at a time when the country was suffering from a serious malady indeed.
Let me say again that this bill is not a price and income control scheme, it is not an anti-inflationary scheme. The fact of the matter is that the economy is sick, there is no question about that, and the measures of that sickness are multiple. One measure is in terms of our trade imbalance.
Earlier a member of the NDP indicated that our trade situation was fine. Obviously he has not examined the figures because, if he did, he would see that in 1975 Canada's trade imbalance in high technology products will be $9 billion as compared to $2 billion five years ago. There has been a steady deterioration over the last five years in our trade imbalance in high technology products. We are partially paying for the $9 billion by selling off capital, selling off part of the farm, and selling our raw materials. That is irresponsible. We simply must become more competitive in high technology production, and anyone who chooses not to see these figures, as does the NDP, is being totally irresponsible.
Another measure of the performance of our economy and the sickness from which it is evidently suffering was provided in this morning's Montreal Gazette in an article written by Mr. Peter Cook. The article is headed "Canadi-
