subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-73 may I say that judging from the status of the bill and the present response of the public to it, we can see it will receive only grudging support. The large group of organized labour, the Canadian Labour Congress, is telling us what they find distasteful in this bill and what they believe is unfair in the controls as they are proposed to be applied, that is, mostly to wage earners. I think they are making very valid points about the impossibility of applying the whole program fairly. On the other hand, profits are to be curtailed severely to 95 per cent of the previous year's average, which raises the question about our need for large capital expenditures in coming years and whether or not we will be worse off than ever. It has been indicated that in many industries profits were low. The stock market will bear this out.
It will give me great pleasure to vote against this bill as I am sure it will accomplish very little and only set the stage for reduced growth in the years ahead. The imposition of controls on the Canadian economy will slow down the economy's recovery without appreciably reducing inflation for at least a year or more.
Speaking to the Conference Board, Mr. Arthur Smith had this to say, as reported in the Globe and Mail of November 20:
Next year's improvement in productivity ... may be one of the lowest in the past 50 years ...

In addition, "the underlying trend rate of productivity may continue to be among the lowest of all the industrially advanced nations in the world," he told a conference on trade competitiveness sponsored by the board.
Next year, "domestic productivity inhibiting factors, including those likely to arise from the anti-inflation program, are likely to make it extremely difficult to achieve quick and substantial domestic productivity gains".
What may make the situation more difficult for Canada is that it may occur at the same time as the exceptionally large current account deficit, which has been shrinking for the past several quarters, starts to widen again. If the latter happens, as historical experience suggests is likely, it could begin before the end of 1976, Dr. Smith said.
What makes the outlook for late 1976 even less promising is the expected high unemployment level and considerable under-utilized capacity that will be present. Also, Canada may at that time be on the verge of an "enormous" buildup in net import requirements for oil.
Behind the recent deterioration in trade competitiveness for Canada are several factors, failure to increase real new investment spending to any significant extent from 1967 to 1972, the long lagged effect of the appreciation of the Canadian dollar in 1970 and the ending of the special advances in productivity under the auto pact.
"A powerful array of depressing Canadian federal and provincial policies (especially regarding taxation and royalty matters) have curbed strong and efficient growth generally in Canadian resource industries."
No one is more to blame than the government for the problems of our resource industries.
Only during the past year with weakened markets, corporate profits that declined, a more competitive import competition and the perception that inflation was producing intolerable distortions, have Canadians begun to raise the issue of job security and the risks of inadequate new job creation in decisive ways.
Even then, "instead of trying to make labour markets and collective bargaining procedures work much more effectively, we have now acted to introduce a control program which even its most ardent supporters can hardly claim will help to make labour markets work better."
Surely this is an indication of what we are up against with these controls. Let us consider what is happening in the United States where there are no controls. Their third quarter growth reached 13 per cent, the strongest rise since 1960. Almost certainly the U.S. recovery will be superior in performance to that of Canada if for no other reason than the extent to which Canadian controls and their application to profits actively discourage the capital investment essential to establish any prolonged recovery.
The effect of limiting profits will be felt further down the road. The effect of controls is to limit any increase in profit and the process discourages investment. The control program takes the income redistribution process a little further at the expense of real corporate growth. For example, a person told me that he had been in business with a partner and liquidated the business, which had considerable capital, and they were waiting to divide it so that they could start a new business. However, under this legislation they will be prevented from doing so and probably will be for a long time if they are ever allowed at some time in the future to take their money out and get going again in another business. This only goes to show that two small individuals in private enterprise are going to be shackled by this legislation for some time to come.
Almost certainly unemployment will increase in the next few years. A study of the possibility of unemployment in the next few years raises certain disturbing questions. A
December 1, 1975

sharp rise from the rate of 5 per cent in June, 1974, to 7,2 per cent in October of this year has been the result of the North American economic slowdown.
It is clear that the combined effect of income controls, debilitating monetary and fiscal policies, and the low utilization rates in U.S. industry provide little optimism for improvement in our unemployment position. All studies indicate that the restrictive fiscal and monetary policies accompanying the income control plan will only stretch out Canada's high unemployment rate problem.
One of the obvious doubts being expressed is whether the controls will be accepted or will work. From the recent meeting with the federal-provincial ministers it seems obvious that provincial spokesmen are critical of the failure of the government to get the program working and to provide some ruling or benchmark. Mr. Darcy McKeough said, "Let's get it cracking." As to whether we shall have provincial boards to monitor prices, we will have to wait until December. The Anti-Inflation Board chairman now says the board will need to employ 300 people instead of the 200 originally planned. The Saskatchewan finance minister suggested that the meeting was not the most productive and called for a surtax on private incomes of more than $30,000 per year, and by doing so has introduced a new form of control.
How is each province going to react to this? Well, according to the Globe and Mail:
The federal legislation provides that the private sector of the economy will come under the federal Anti-Inflation Board. A province may, according to Ottawa, place its public sector-civil servants, municipal workers, teachers and so on-under the control of the same board. Or it may decide to set up its own board to handle them.
As Quebec has done.
Last week Premier Peter Lougheed told the Alberta legislature, "We concur with the Government of Quebec". He believes that the federal legislation, unsupported by provincial legislation, could constitute an intrusion into the provincial jurisdiction. He fears this on economic as well as constitutional grounds.
Once the federal controls are in place, he fears that they might be kept in place too long, permitting Ottawa to interfere with business to the detriment of economic health.
What Alberta proposes to do, therefore, is to pass legislation that is identical to the federal legislation, with its own additions. The legislation would authorize the lieutenant-governor in council to delegate administration of the act, for both private and public sectors, to Ottawa on a trial basis. Alberta would retain the power to opt out if it found the federal program unsatisfactory, or if Ottawa were to make significant unilateral changes to the program. The unilateral changes which would concern Mr. Lougheed would be anything that put controls on prices of products at the farm gate or further controls on petroleum products.
They put on a time limit of 18 months, which I think is in line with what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has suggested, that controls should be re-examined at the end of 18 months. All this indicates that the public is becoming unhappy with the program and is seeing that it is in fact Swiss cheese, with so many holes that in effect it is not a program at all.
The growing confusion in the five weeks since the time of the announcement on October 13 is overwhelming, and the Leader of the Opposition has had this to say:
The government can bring in whatever kind of controls program it chooses within the ranges of these wide powers; it can vary any program virtually beyond recognition while the law remains in effect.- It asked us to accept instead a complicated review process which, in
Anti-Inflation Act
effect, represents nothing more than a progress report to be followed by a vote which would be meaningless considering the government's majority strength in the Commons.
This is the great problem with this program at a time when confederation is indicating to all that there is too much centralization in the economy and in the political process. We are going to centralize further with an army of civil servants.
It is obvious that Mrs. Plumptre, as a member of the Anti-Inflation Board and being critical of the action of the Egg Marketing Agency in raising the price of eggs at a time when feed costs were dropping, touched a very sensitive nerve with consumers. It is obvious that the board can do nothing about farm gate prices. I do not see it being able to do so unless it wants to have shortages develop very quickly. It is estimated that 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the change in food prices is related to farm gate prices for food consumed within our own country. That merely leaves the Anti-Inflation Board with the possibility of doing something about food from the time it leaves the farm gate until it ends up in the housewife's basket, and that would be precious little. Indeed, a substantial amount of foods is imported.
Labour is unhappy with the program; what about management? Mr. J. L. Biddell has expressed the view that the proposed guidelines are too tough on business. There is a comment by Mr. R. W. Billingsley, president of the Reed Paper company, who said in Toronto last week:
"Perhaps the best thing I can say about the policy as now proposed is that it probably won't work, which means that it will have little detrimental effect on the economy."
Billingsley's comments about the program point to one fallacy-that the control program is supported by business but opposed by labor.
I suggest that many businessmen are concerned about the long-term effects of the program on business. These effects can only be endured for a short time, if there are not to be serious consequences to productivity and investment. And nobody believes that the government is seriously concerned about cutting public expenditures. Indeed, the setting up of the bilingual districts, announced a few days ago, can be cited as an example of the government's intentions.
The government's campaign has lost support for the control program, rather than rallying support. Canadians are not willing to support this sort of program. They do not want to hear the Prime Minister talking about a wartime atmosphere; neither do they like Premier Regan's reference to the Dunkirk spirit. We are not ready for it. Even the Prime Minister has said that the program is primarily psychological, not economic. Canadians really do not believe that controls will work in peacetime. Organized labour has been portrayed as being against this program, while business has been portrayed as supporting it. But there are many misgivings in the business community about the value of the plan. Businessmen believe that, in the long run, it will do considerably more harm than good.
This controls plan is really a ploy in that the federal government is trying to shift the problem to the private sector from the public sector where most of it belongs. Without doubt, if inflation is to be curtailed there must be a drastic reduction, at least in the rate of government

December 1, 1975
Anti-Inflation Act
spending, and a corresponding contraction in the money supply. The number of claims for exemption from the guidelines which will qualify for special treatment within the incomes policy will be much greater than we can expect.
I cannot help but agree with much that was said in the Canadian Labour Congress brief to the finance committee. The congress maintains that the federal government has been largely responsible, through the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada which has been developed in a most erratic fashion, for it swings from one extreme to the other. Monetary policy has never been stable, and this has created economic instability of serious proportions. All kinds of cost pressures were built into the economy from the blatant mismanagement of our monetary policy. The congress went on to say that the mismanagement of fiscal policy has been almost as bad.
The Federal Reserve Board of the United States has tried to hold the expansion of the United States money supply to some 5 per cent. In Canada the position is somewhat different. Governor Bouey has gone to great lengths to explain that the chief problem with monetary policy lies in making sure it is the right policy. He suggests that we need a moderate rate of monetary expansion, sufficient to support rising levels of economic activity, together with a gradual decline in the rate of inflation. He asked what constitutes a moderate and sufficient rate of monetary growth, and suggested that the Central Bank has been too vague in defining its goals. Others, while applauding objectives underlying the control of the money supply, are unhappy about the effect of monetary restrictions on interest rates.
Mr. Bouey has pointed out that in the past two years our money supply has expanded at an annual rate of 15 per cent, although at the end of the second quarter in 1975 the rate of expansion had been brought down to 10 per cent. Weekly statistics published by the Bank of Canada show that the money supply, as defined by Mr. Bouey, rose by 17.5 per cent, from October, 1974 to October 1975; in the past six months, from the end of April, the money supply increased by 15.8 per cent, while in the last three months the rate of increase was at 15.6 per cent. This indicates that the expansion of our money supply is proceeding apace, with no indication that it is coming down to the sort of figure the Americans have in mind.
In their brief the Canadian Labour Congress set out what the program is not able to do, namely, come to grips with the weight of external factors which produce inflationary pressures on our open economy. The government has conceded that the prices of imported products will not be controlled and that this will continue to be a major inflationary influence on Canadian costs and prices. As the world around us slowly recovers from recession, it really means that the price of foreign goods will rise. This will constitute a large element in the increase of prices in Canada. I believe that this will be the single most important factor which will prevent this program from having an over-all effect on the rate of inflation in this country.
We are now attempting, Mr. Speaker, to apply a form of wage and price control which proved wanting when applied in the United States and the United Kingdom. Shortages are bound to occur. When they do, people hoard.

Scarce goods are stockpiled and the shortage is compounded.
Various countries, even provinces and cities in Canada, have tried rent controls on residential housing. Always such controls have brought the people close to disaster and created shortages. The government has tossed this knotty problem to the provinces. When rents are controlled for any length, investment is discouraged. Continuous acrimonious debates go on between landlord and tenant, and nobody is happy. One of the great problems in controlled rents is arriving at a reasonable rent increase. The tenants, naturally, ask for reduced rents, and landlords for increased rents. As there are many more tenants than landlords there is a marked tendency for boards to keep rents below economic levels. We tend to become penny wise and pound foolish and, eventually, shortages develop.
This bill will not cure inflation, and may even compound it. It will almost certainly increase unemployment in the 18 months or so it will operate, by stifling productivity. Obviously, professionals will have to pare and reduce their workload in order not to breach the guidelines because, if they do, even with increased productivity, they will find themselves penalized. The large number of employees working for the 1,500 firms covered by the guidelines will feel aggrieved when comparing their lot with that of workers in firms not covered. Clearly, their fellow workers will have greater advantages when seeking wage increases. This can only accentuate the harmful effects which changing inflationary conditions can exert on the Canadian economy.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, is no substitute for good control of the money supply, reasonable fiscal measures and, above all, prudent government spending. Unless we wish to have a completely controlled economy, these standard and traditional methods are still the best means for controlling an economy in a free society.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESTRAINT OF PROFIT MARGINS, PRICES, DIVIDENDS AND COMPENSATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to register my opposition to this bill on third reading I begin by saying that we have opposed this bill from the beginning because we argue, and our arguments are supported by virtually all economists except those bought by the government, that this so-called anti-inflation program cannot work.
The government calls this a bill "to provide for the restraint of profit margins, prices, dividends and compensation in Canada." All available evidence, reports of discussions of provincial governments with the minister and the buffoon chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, as well as statements of the Anti-Inflation Board, reinforce our view that this program could not have worked from its conception, which was illegitimate, one might say. In addition, if one considers the composition of the board, what it has accomplished, said, and refused to say until now, one thing becomes apparent-this board will not deal with the problems suggested by the title of the bill; at least it will not deal with them equitably. It will not restrain profit margins, freeze prices, hold back dividends, etc. It will do one job only-restrain wages and salaries.
Look at the board's membership. Its chairman, just a dozen or so years ago, was a professor in a Canadian university, probably making not more than $10,000 a year.
December 1, 1975

He was elected as a member of parliament, became a minister, and was defeated in 1972. He immediately became a lobbyist for multi-national and large national corporations. He has now been appointed as chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board at a salary of more than $50,000 a year. By his own admission he is taking a cut in income. We can see on what side his bread is buttered.
The vice-chairman, Mrs. Plumptre, receives $40,000 a year. As Chairman of the Food Prices Review Board she received a lot of press coverage. However, very few in the press gallery seemed to do much other than read the headlines. They did not read the reports that were made. They did not read the fine print.
Let us look at Mrs. Plumptre's record. After looking at price increases for butter, eggs, meat, and everything else, what did she tell the Canadian public? She said the farmers are receiving too much for their products. Workers in British Columbia's supermarkets asked for wage increases which she said are too high. She said they are responsible for high prices.
Every time Mrs. Plumptre looked at food processors such as Canada Packers, Burns or Swift, she assured the public that they were not making too much money and that everything was fine. Even though their profits have gone up every year, she says they are legitimate profits.
Then there are the supermarkets which are growing in number, dollar volume, and profits every year. After looking at them she said that Loblaws, Safeway and Dominion Stores were not making too much money. She said it was the farmer and the supermarket worker who were getting too much. They are the villains.
We then come to the former vice-president of Clarkson Company. I thought the board would have at least given the appearance of being impartial. I thought the board would at least seem to be fair and look at all the questions before giving a judgment. I quote from the November 19, 1975, issue of the Globe and Mail where Mr. Biddell, the former vice-president of Clarkson Company said, and I quote:
"The regulations are likely to be too restrictive and inflexible and I would expect an early need for adjustment."
The regulations have not even been tabled. They may have been drafted, but they are being kept secret. Mr. Biddell, however, knows that they are too restrictive. I again quote from the article:
He envisages a system where a company's auditors, as part of their normal function of verifying financial statements, would also take on the additional responsibility of ensuring obedience to the wage and price guidelines.
The auditors for Eaton's, Hudson Bay Mining, Swift and Company, who receive their salaries from those companies, will work for the government, at no cost to the government, protecting the interests of the ordinary people! I know whose interests Mr. Biddell has, and they are not the interests of the Canadian people. It is the interests of his former corporate clients. I again quote:
Adjournment Motion
"The white paper guidelines will require the businessman to suppress almost every one of his natural entrepreneurial drives." . ..
The program's effect on wage and salary earners will not be severe, he said. "I think they will get along quite well."
I am sure the teachers in Toronto agree with Mr. Biddell today.
We then have a man who took a job that no other labour leader would look at. Not a single labour union has given its approval to the program. The CBC tried to tell the public that the CBRT and the Public Service Alliance had endorsed the guidelines. What they said was that they would support some kind of wage restraint if there were price controls which, of course, the minister has rejected from the beginning.
The former vice-president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Ladyman, has gone from being vice-president of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, a union which has been very successful in getting high wages for its members, and I give it credit for that, to being a consultant for the great friend of the working people, Great West Life Insurance, an affiliate of that poor powerless corporation, Power Corporation. No other labour person would go anywhere near the program, but Mr. Ladyman did. I suggest he had good reason.
Let us look at what this board has done in its short existence. The board issued a statement in November saying that it was not the intention of the board to replace the collective bargaining process. It said it was expected that the parties would negotiate in good faith with a view to concluding an agreement under the guidelines. After they had reached an agreement, the board said it would then look at the agreement to see if in fact it was too high.
It was only a couple of weeks ago that that policy was laid down. The board has already violated its own statement. In the case of the Toronto teachers the board acted before there was an agreement. The board acted at the request of one of the contestants. I say that the chairman and the board showed their bias. They showed it further this week by saying not one word about the exorbitant, fantastic profits which the large Canadian banks have reported this year.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTION THAT MINISTERS BE PRESENT AT NATIONAL CONFERENCES RELATED TO THE ATLANTIC FISHERY
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTION THAT MINISTERS BE PRESENT AT NATIONAL CONFERENCES RELATED TO THE ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 22, as recorded at page 7803 of Hansard, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question with regard to the level of representation which the government would make at all future meetings in which we would negotiate our position in respect to the Law of the Sea, ICNAF and so on. The answer I received when I asked that the ministerial level be the level at which we should be represented was, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I will note the hon. member's representation.
I suppose the day of debate for this could not have been more timely than this evening. Today I received a call from a fisherman. He advises me that in one of the areas off the Atlantic coast the Russian fleet has a quota of 19,000 tons. The Russian fleet appeared in that zone in May, 1975. It is present still, and it is still fishing. As to the 19,000 ton quota, I might say to you, Mr. Speaker, that two good-sized boats operating off the Atlantic Coast would be quite adequate to catch that quota of fish in a much shorter period than that between May and December.
There is, on the Atlantic coast, absolutely no trust that the foreign fleets are observing the quotas. Negotiations have taken place on an international basis, as we know, and we must compliment Mr. Beasley who has headed these negotiations on many occasions and who is, unquestionably, a very able and dedicated Canadian. The trouble is that whether or not he is scared of the minister, as has just been suggested by one of my hon. friends, or whether or not the minister gives him proper authority, the negotiations have not been as productive as they should have been. Attending these meetings, one finds that able people are sent by other governments-representatives who are capable of making decisions on the spot.
The only way in which Canada can hope to be represented by someone authorized to make decisions on the spot with respect to the welfare of our offshore fleet is by the minister responsible for the fisheries being a member of the negotiating team at all times. First, this would give us decision-making ability. Second, and at least as important, the presence of the minister would confer a prestige upon the delegation which it would not otherwise possess. Thus far, we have given an indication to all the foreign countries concerned with which we have been negotiating that these are items of secondary importance at best because the minister has never been present to negotiate.
This matter has been brought up on a number of occasions. If we look at page 7804 of Hansard we find the Prime Minister in reply to the hon. member for Annapolis Valley

(Mr. Nowlan) saying, in effect, that it is difficult to withdraw historic fishing rights from European nations which have fished off our coasts for hundreds of years. I want to point out that until we entered upon this complex of international negotiations and treaties we encountered no problem as far as nations with historic fishing rights, such as Portugal and Britain, were concerned. However when we began to carve the pie up among a multitude of international fishing fleets, when we started to extend the use of these waters to Germany, East Germany, Russia, Poland, Japan, etc., the depradation of the seas began.
The Prime Minister also suggested in one of his answers on this subject-these are his words-"Of course we trust them; that was why we would not let the Russian ships come into the ports." That is a strange statement for a prime minister to make. We trust them, so we won't let them enter our ports. We are in a serious position.
The fishermen in the herring industry find that they are constrained by international agreement to the point where they can no longer make a living. The halibut and haddock fishermen are dumping their fish at sea because they dare not come ashore with them.
It is high time that the government took its stand strongly and clearly and that we, as a country, assert our historic rights; that we as a coastal state have jurisdiction over these resources; that we have our minister or the Prime Minister himself so express ourselves in the international meetings in order to bring back to this country the opportunity for making a livelihood for our fishermen off our shores, as well as for the processors and workers on shore. Let us exercise our historic rights in the fishing industry and supply the world with the food it so badly needs.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SUGGESTION THAT MINISTERS BE PRESENT AT NATIONAL CONFERENCES RELATED TO THE ATLANTIC FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to the comments of the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) basically because, as he pointed out in his initial remarks, his original question was put on July 22, which by some strange coincidence was immediately after the ICNAF meeting in Edinburgh, Scotland, in June of 1975.
I suggest that at the time he put his question the hon. member did not expect the eventual success that was reached by the negotiators, including the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc), at the meeting completed in September of 1975 in Montreal. It is of interest to note that during the subsequent negotiations the minister was successful in reaching most of the aims that he had set himself in June. He succeeded in having the foreign fishing fleets of nations belonging to ICNAF, including the Russians, Spaniards, Portuguese, Germans, French and so on, limit their fishing efforts by 40 per cent. In that he achieved aims that members opposite did not think would be possible.
I think the compliments that the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte paid to the negotiator should have been directed to the Minister of State (Fisheries), who has manifested in his portfolio imagination and persuasiveness, and has sought to protect the interests of the very fishermen in whom the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte has displayed interest.
December 1, 1975

With reference to the herring fishery, I suggest that there has to be a recognition on the part of the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. If we are to study the fishing stocks and the quality and condition of those fish stocks through ICNAF, there has to be as well on the part of Canadians a conscientiousness and an awareness of the necessity for preservation and building up of fish stocks. If we do enter into international relations whereby foreign fishing fleets limit their catch, Canadians must also be mindful of conservation and the development of fish stocks.
I thank the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte for communicating to the House the information he has received from one fisherman in his riding. I suggest we all communicate that information to the Minister of State (Fisheries), who in the past has shown a great deal of dispatch in dealing with such matters and investigating and taking appropriate action. The hon. member's reference to the action relating to the Russian fishing fleet is a case in point.

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-STRIKE OF PULP AND PAPER WORKERS-RESULTS OF DISCUSSION WITH COMPANIES- SUGGESTION ANTI-INFLATION BOARD BE FLEXIBLE
LABOUR CONDITIONS-STRIKE OF PULP AND PAPER WORKERS-RESULTS OF DISCUSSION WITH COMPANIES- SUGGESTION ANTI-INFLATION BOARD BE FLEXIBLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I could elaborate on the last question, but I am pleased that I can elaborate on a question that I put to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) in this House today having to do with the pulp and paper industry.
For some reason or other, I will never understand in a million years why we do not take up in the House of Commons matters of concern to Canadians, rather than items that are newsworthy in the eyes of the press gallery. We should deal with situations of concern to the Canadian economy. I wonder why the Canadian Press has someone in the press gallery even at this time to bother making notes, because they do not pay any bloody attention to what goes on in the House of Commons. They are concerned with what might be sensational and what that can do to some newspapers.
The pulp and paper industry stands second in manufacturing capacity in the world with a total of 1,290,000 workers. I got these figures from Statistics Canada today. In Canada the industry supports 61,873 production workers, or 5 per cent of the total in the pulp and paper industry.
The industry is the second largest in Canada. There are 41 pulp and paper mills on downtime and many more are being added each day as a result of strikes. This pulp and paper industry which is so vital to our economy is going to drive our economy into disaster and drive Canadian exports into oblivion.
Of total world exports of pulp and paper, Canada's exports are responsible for 7 million, or the greatest percentage of the pulp and paper industry exports of some 11 million. The main thrust of my question tonight is related to the effect of strike action in the Atlantic region, particularly in the province of Newfoundland, where the pulp and
Adjournment Motion
paper industry, apart from the fishing industry, is the basis of our economy.
Already two paper mills in Corner Brook and Grand Falls, and a linerboard mill in Stephenville are oh strike. This is the whole basis of the economy of Newfoundland, and these strikes affect some 3,525 employees, not taking into account ancillary employment in resulting services. If we were to take into account the two and a half times factor that results we would be talking about the jobs of some 9,000 employees in a province where the unemployment rate is over 19.6 per cent. If we add the 28,000 unemployed, this would bring the percentage much higher.
In 1973 the total number of workers in production capacity was just over 11,000, and of this number some 2,590, or one-quarter of that force, were in the pulp and paper industry. This figure has now reached 3,525 in three mills, which is approaching the one-third level. When taking into account our total work force it is obvious that this situation is more than disastrous.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) indicated today in his answer to me that the responsibility in so far as coming to terms between industries and unions is concerned was of provincial nature. I quarrel with the minister's determination in this regard. When any breakdown is in such a vital industry that it is of national priority in its influence, surely it has to be treated as a national responsibility, not only from a labour point of view but from the point of view of a declaration of responsibility by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie).
I feel that a responsibility exists in relation to the AntiInflation Board, particularly when it is difficult to determine responsibility from the point of view of the guidelines laid down and negotiations between management and labour as related to the October 14 deadline.
It should be obvious that, as both the minister and I projected today, in the Atlantic region which is so dependent on the pulp and paper industry, the embarrassing unemployment rate should demand some concern, particularly when there appears to be a total collapse of the industry in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia.
It is, therefore, most glaringly obvious that when the difficulties exist in an industry with that basis in the Atlantic region, in light of the effect as declared by the Irving settlement, the situation must be examined on the basis of a uniform agreement throughout the region regarding all aspects of pulp and paper mills in Atlantic Canada.
Alternately, Madam Speaker, we can look at the facts as they reflect the situation in the whole of the Atlantic region where not only is the unemployment rate the highest in Canada, but where the New Brunswick and the Irving situation are prevalent and where the entire pulp and paper industry in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia is in a state of complete collapse. If in fact this situation is recognized then it is incumbent not only on the Minister of Labour, who I am sure is most sympathetic, but also on the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), and the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board, to exercise the necessary flexibility in determining the guidelines die-

December 1, 1975
Adjournment Motion
tated by the anti-inflation memoranda so that a state of justice can be recognized in order to determine justice for all.
I hope that the representative of the minister in replying tonight will recognize that the pulp and paper industry has an influence on the Canadian export trade, and that therefore the Government of Canada should take steps to resolve this problem which affects so many people in our work force.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-STRIKE OF PULP AND PAPER WORKERS-RESULTS OF DISCUSSION WITH COMPANIES- SUGGESTION ANTI-INFLATION BOARD BE FLEXIBLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) for raising a question which is so important to more than 60,000 Canadian employees, as he said himself.

The government fully understands and shares the concern voiced by members of this House on the gravity of the work stoppages facing the pulp and paper industry. As members will appreciate, while this industry is one of national importance it nevertheless is one which falls for labour relations purposes under the provinces in which it is located. Members will be aware that several provincial ministers of labour are faced with work stoppages within their respective jurisdiction in this important industry. These ministers and their officials are, of course, working to encourage settlements in the disputes, and remain in close touch with developments in each of the particular cases.
As the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) pointed out in the house earlier, he has not received any notification directly from the companies following request for them to review negotiations. However, as he also pointed out, a settlement has been reached in the Saint John area relatively recently. According to reports, about 500 members of the Canadian Paper Workers' Union employed by Irving Pulp and Paper Limited of Saint John, New Brunswick, have ratified a two-year contract which would renew one expiring last April.
Questions have been asked by members of this House concerning the need for the Anti-Inflation Board to indicate whether or not the settlement reached in this case might be used as a benchmark in other cases. As the Minister of Labour pointed out, it is not his function to tell the board what it should be doing which individual settlements. Indeed, it would be quite contrary and prejudicial to the board's independent status for him to do so. However, he has indicated that the workers may be entitled to more money because unions which entered negotiation for new contracts before the guidelines were proclaimed October 14, and whose previous collective agreement was signed before January 1,	1974, could get special
consideration.
It cannot be stressed too strongly that parties to disputes in the pulp and paper industry, and indeed parties to collective bargaining disputes generally, should not pass the responsibility to the Anti-Inflation Board or the Minister of Labour. They have a responsibility to bargain together in good faith to secure settlements. Labour departments in all jurisdictions have experienced personnel

available to assist them should the need arise. The AntiInflation Board, in spite of its relatively brief existence, is gearing up to answer technical questions for the application of the guidelines, and has guaranteed an answer within 30 days.
Hon. members may be assured that the government will continue to watch developments in this important industry very closely. It must be remembered, however, that we live in a free society, and among the freedoms valued very highly are the freedom of association and the right to bargain collectively.
It seems that at the present time some employers abuse the guidelines and refuse to sit down at the negotiation table, obviously failing to meet their responsibilities towards their employees. We want to correct this situation as soon as possible.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ANGOLA-POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT ACTION AT UNITED NATIONS TO PREVENT FOREIGN INTERVENTION IN CONFLICT
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ANGOLA-POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT ACTION AT UNITED NATIONS TO PREVENT FOREIGN INTERVENTION IN CONFLICT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 17 I raised a question with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) regarding representations that might be made by Canada concerning the situation developing in Angola. At that time the minister said that no initiatives had been taken. In the reply tonight I will probably be told that subsequent to my question representations have been made at the UN. But that is not really sufficient. I would appreciate the opportunity to enlarge somewhat on my question.
I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs has taken an extraordinary interest in Angola for some time. On February 19, 1975, addressing the fifth annual conference of the Canadian Association of African Studies in Toronto he said:
Developments in Southern Africa during the last year give some hope that the situation may significantly improve. Events in the Portuguese territories have been so rapid and so dramatic that they emphasize how unwise it is to be dogmatic. We are gratified and encouraged by the decolonization process undertaken by the Portuguese government. Very few people foresaw such changes as have occurred in Guinea Bissau, Angola and Mozambique during the past year.
Then he went on to point out the pressures that have been placed on South Africa to change its policies.
On April 11 the minister announced that Canada would be sending a special diplomatic mission to Angola and Mozambique, two Portuguese African territories which were scheduled to become independent later this year. The mission, which was to take place from May 5 to 26, was intended primarily to make a first contact with the provisional governments and future leaders of these countries. One may wonder why a mission was being sent so early and prior to their actual independence, but if we read the announcement of April 24 we learn why. Speaking in Accra the minister said:
... and we are sending in the next few weeks a special mission to Angola and Mozambique to lay the ground for good relations with these countries, as well as the smaller Portuguese territories of Africa, which
December 1, 1975

will stand as free and sovereign members of the United Nations and the OAU.
We learn there was a reason for that special mission. Then, on November 13, we had a somewhat belated and wan announcement which reads:
Canada has consistently supported the rights of colonized peoples to self-determination and independence, and we have accordingly taken note and welcomed Angola's independence from Portugal which took place on November 11. However, the political and security situations there are extremely confused, and we are not at present in a position to recognize or enter into relations with any group which may claim to govern the country.
One may wonder just what report the special mission brought back. It seems to me, now we are hearing disquieting stories about Soviet and Cuban interventions, and about intervention from Zaire and intervention from South Africa, there should be a flurry of diplomatic activity to match the flurry that has gone on, and the minister's interest now should continue and not suddenly fade, when surely this is the time for Canada to be interested in a situation which very seriously threatens the peace of the world.
I would inquire what representations, not only in the UN but directly to the nations involved, the minister has made, or whether any pressure was put on Cuba. It seems to me that through our long ties with that country this is the place where some influence should have been built up over recent years. What representations have been made to the Soviet Union or to Zaire? Surely with our interest in western Africa through many years a certain influence should have been built up. If we have been pressuring South Africa, what questions have been asked there about the situation developing in Angola?
Surely if the minister has been so interested I cannot believe that the special mission did not come back without some very serious warnings to him. I cannot believe that he was not in a position months ago to have voiced the fear that there would be foreign interventions in Angola, and that a very explosive situation would develop there.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-ANGOLA-POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT ACTION AT UNITED NATIONS TO PREVENT FOREIGN INTERVENTION IN CONFLICT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for drawing the attention of the House to such an important matter. Evidently, it is an extremely difficult question, especially in an underdeveloped continent such as Africa where most countries have been independent only since 1960. The experience of almost all
Adjournment Motion
countries, especially in South Africa, not the country itself but the southern area of that continent, leaves much room for improvement. They obviously need much sympathy and understanding from all countries. This sympathy and understanding were apparent from the beginning in the minister's statement.

As the hon. member indicated at the outset, when Angola contemplated independence the minister indicated the government's position that there was a hope that upon the granting of independence there could be a recognition within a short period of time. That is always hoped for. Unfortunately, as the political situation developed, it became evident that there were conflicting positions taken by various groups within Angola itself. The minister indicated that because of that political uncertainty, upon the declaration of independence if there was any possibility on the part of Canada to make any decision on a de jure or de facto recognition-Canada recognizing that Africa is not an area with which Canada is overly familiar-Canada could not play any helpful role by direct intervention or even in direct intervention in any of the affairs of the countries involved in this particular dispute.
However, Canada has always offered its assistance in the ways it felt it would be helpful to the nations concerned. Canada has repeatedly contributed to the International Red Cross and answered its appeals for the victims of the strife, and has indicated its preparedness to continue doing so.
I note from the remarks of the hon. member that he has been very interested in the pronouncements made by the minister relating to Angola. However, in listening to the minister's words being repeated in this House I find that there is nothing there which is contradictory, or anything which could be held to be negative or which would indicate that Canada is not ready to accept its international responsibilities. I suggest that before Canada can take bilateral steps, unilateral steps, or any steps through the United Nations, it has to think very seriously of the consequences. I think that to date the position Canada has adopted is one which ought to be commended.
